mock1.t: Fall protection — low-slope roof, narrow building
mock1.q: A three-person crew is tearing off and replacing a built-up roof on a flat (¼:12) roof that is 42 ft wide and 120 ft long. The edges are 28 ft above grade. No mechanical equipment will be used. Which fall-protection approach is permitted by itself, without any other system?
o: A warning line system set 6 ft from all edges
Toeboards installed along every roof edge
A safety monitoring system with a competent-person monitor
Having workers stay at least 10 ft from the edge whenever possible
mock1.e: For roofing work on low-slope roofs, 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(10) allows a safety monitoring system alone when the roof is 50 ft or less in width. This roof is 42 ft wide, so a monitor alone is permitted.

w.0: A warning line only marks an area. It must be combined with guardrails, nets, PFAS, or a safety monitor, because work still happens between the line and the edge.
w.1: Toeboards protect people below from falling objects. They do not stop a worker from falling.
w.3: "Stay back when possible" is not a fall-protection system recognized by OSHA.

mock1.q: A crew is reroofing a two-story house with a 7:12 slope. The eaves are 19 ft above grade. Which is the BEST fall protection for this job?
o: Personal fall arrest systems attached to roof anchors fastened into the framing per the anchor manufacturer's instructions
A warning line along the eaves combined with a safety monitor
A safety monitor who watches all workers from the ground
Roof brackets with a 2×6 slide guard at the eave, and no other protection
mock1.e: A 7:12 roof is a steep roof (greater than 4:12). Steep roofs require guardrails with toeboards, safety nets, or PFAS (1926.501(b)(11)). For residential construction (1926.501(b)(13)), conventional protection is presumed feasible. PFAS on properly installed anchors is the standard, compliant choice.

w.1: Warning lines and safety monitors are only permitted for roofing work on low-slope roofs (4:12 or less).
w.2: A monitor must be on the same walking/working surface as the workers, and monitors aren't permitted on steep roofs anyway.
w.3: Slide guards alone are not an OSHA fall-protection system. The old interim residential guidance that allowed them was rescinded.

mock1.q: A mechanical felt-laying machine will travel east–west on a low-slope roof. How far from the east and west roof edges, which are perpendicular to the machine's direction of travel, must the warning line be at minimum?
o: 6 ft
8 ft
10 ft
15 ft
mock1.e: When mechanical equipment is used, the warning line must be at least 6 ft from edges parallel to the direction of travel and at least 10 ft from edges perpendicular to it. The machine could run straight toward those edges.

w.0: 6 ft is the distance for edges parallel to travel, or for work with no mechanical equipment.
w.1: 8 ft is not a value in the warning-line rule.
w.3: 15 ft exceeds the minimum. It is allowed, but it is not the required minimum.

mock1.q: A foreman inspects a newly erected warning line. Which condition violates OSHA's warning-line requirements?
o: The stanchions resist a 20-lb horizontal push applied 30 in above the roof without tipping
The rope sags to 31 in above the roof surface between two stanchions
The line is flagged with high-visibility material every 5 ft
The line's highest point is 38 in above the roof surface
mock1.e: The line's lowest point, including sag, must be no less than 34 in above the walking/working surface, and its highest point no more than 39 in. A 31-in sag is too low.

w.0: Stanchions must resist at least 16 lb at 30 in, so 20 lb exceeds the requirement.
w.2: Flagging is required at intervals of not more than 6 ft, so 5 ft complies.
w.3: 38 in is within the 34–39 in range.

mock1.t: PFAS — anchorage location and free fall
mock1.q: A roofer wears a full-body harness with a 6-ft shock-absorbing lanyard. The lanyard is clipped to a roof anchor at the level of the roofer's feet on a 6:12 roof. What is the MAIN problem with this setup?
o: Lanyards must never be used on steep roofs
There is no problem, because the shock absorber reduces the arresting force
The anchor must be rated for 1,800 lb
The potential free fall is about 11 ft, which exceeds OSHA's 6-ft free-fall limit
mock1.e: With the anchor at foot level, the worker falls the lanyard length plus the height of the back D-ring (about 5 ft) before the lanyard even starts to arrest: roughly 11 ft. A PFAS must be rigged so free fall is no more than 6 ft and the worker cannot contact a lower level. Fixes include an overhead or ridge anchor with a shorter connection, or a self-retracting lifeline or lanyard rated for foot-level anchorage.

w.0: Lanyards are allowed on steep roofs when the PFAS is rigged correctly.
w.1: A shock absorber limits the arresting force, but it does not cure excess free fall or the risk of hitting a lower level.
w.2: 1,800 lb is the maximum arresting force on the worker, not the anchorage strength. Anchorage is 5,000 lb per worker, or designed with a safety factor of 2 by a qualified person.

mock1.q: A roofer slips, and his PFAS stops the fall. He is uninjured and is quickly helped back onto the roof. What should happen to his harness and lanyard?
o: Remove them from service until a competent person inspects them and determines they are undamaged
The worker may put them back on if he sees no visible damage
Continue using them for the rest of the shift, then send them for inspection
Replace only the lanyard; harnesses are not affected by a fall
mock1.e: Components subjected to impact loading must be removed from service immediately. They may not be used again until a competent person inspects them and determines they are undamaged and suitable for reuse. Many manufacturers require destroying equipment that arrested a fall.

w.1: The worker is not necessarily a competent person, and internal damage may not be visible.
w.2: Continued use after an arrest is exactly what the rule prohibits.
w.3: Harness webbing and stitching can also be damaged in an arrest.

mock1.q: A PFAS anchorage is not designed by a qualified person. What minimum load must it support per employee attached?
mock1.e: Anchorages for PFAS must support at least 5,000 lb per employee attached. The alternative is an anchorage designed, installed, and used as part of a complete PFAS with a safety factor of at least two, under the supervision of a qualified person.

w.0: 1,800 lb is the maximum arresting force allowed on the body with a harness.
w.1: 3,000 lb applies to self-retracting lifelines that limit free fall to 2 ft or less, and to positioning-device anchorages.
w.2: 3,600 lb is the proof-test load for snaphooks and D-rings.

mock1.q: Crew members will work near several plastic dome skylights while replacing a low-slope roof. How should the skylights be protected?
o: The domes are adequate if they are polycarbonate rather than acrylic
With covers or screens able to support at least twice the imposed load, or with guardrails around them, or by PFAS
By painting the curbs a high-visibility color
With a warning line set 6 ft from each skylight
mock1.e: Skylights are treated as holes. Employees must be protected from falling through them by covers, guardrails, or PFAS. Covers must support at least twice the weight of the employees, equipment, and materials that may be imposed, and must be secured and marked.

w.0: A skylight dome is not a cover, and falls through domes are a leading cause of roofing deaths.
w.2: Marking a curb is a warning, not fall protection.
w.3: Warning lines are not a permitted protection for holes.

mock1.q: No guardrails are erected at the edge of a low-slope roof. During roofing work, how close to the edge may rolls and insulation be stored?
o: No closer than 4 ft
No closer than 6 ft
No closer than 10 ft
No closer than 15 ft
mock1.e: During roofing work, materials and equipment may not be stored within 6 ft of a roof edge unless guardrails are erected at the edge.

w.0: 4 ft is the storage distance used for overhand bricklaying, a different operation.
w.2: 10 ft relates to warning lines perpendicular to mechanical equipment travel, not storage.
w.3: 15 ft is not the rule, though storing farther back is permitted.

mock1.q: Tear-off debris must get from a roof edge 25 ft above grade to a dumpster outside the building's exterior wall. Which method complies with OSHA?
o: Dropping the debris into a barricaded area 6 ft from the wall
Throwing the debris into the dumpster, with a ground-level spotter
An enclosed chute to the dumpster
Dropping the debris after bagging it in contractor bags
mock1.e: When material is dropped more than 20 ft to any point outside the exterior walls of a building, an enclosed chute must be used.

w.0: Barricades (at least 42 in high and 6 ft back from the opening) apply when debris is dropped through holes in floors without chutes, not from roofs over 20 ft outside the walls.
w.1: A spotter does not replace the chute requirement.
w.3: Bagging does not change the drop-height rule.

mock1.q: An extension ladder leans against a gutter line 20 ft above level ground. Using OSHA's 4-to-1 rule, how far from the wall should the base of the ladder be?
o: 3 ft
4 ft
5 ft
6 ft 8 in
mock1.e: The horizontal distance from the top support to the foot should be about one-quarter of the working length. That is commonly figured as one-quarter of the height to the support point: 20 ft ÷ 4 = 5 ft. The ladder rails must also extend 3 ft above the landing.

w.0: 3 ft is too steep, and the ladder could tip backward.
w.1: 4 ft would be correct for a 16-ft support height.
w.3: 6 ft 8 in is a 3-to-1 ratio. That is too shallow, and the base could kick out.

mock1.q: A worker must set a ladder where it could contact the service drop to the house. Which ladder choice is correct?
o: A wooden ladder, which is always safe near energized lines
A Type IA aluminum ladder, if it is tied off at the top
A ladder with nonconductive (e.g., fiberglass) side rails, set and used so that clearance from the line is maintained
An aluminum ladder with rubber feet, which insulate it from ground
mock1.e: Portable ladders must have nonconductive side rails if they are used where the employee or the ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment. Clearance from lines must still be maintained.

w.0: Wood can conduct when wet or dirty. "Always safe" is false, and wood ladders are rarely used by roofers.
w.1: Duty rating and tying off do not make aluminum nonconductive.
w.3: Rubber feet do not insulate the rails. Current flows through the worker.

mock1.q: On a construction site, which of these needs ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection (or an assured equipment grounding conductor program)?
o: A temporary 120-volt, 20-amp receptacle the crew uses for saws and a compressor
A 480-volt three-phase disconnect serving a rooftop unit
A cordless drill's battery charger that is plugged into a GFCI outlet
The building's permanent wiring, which is not being used by the crew
mock1.e: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle outlets on construction sites that are not part of the permanent wiring and are in use by employees must have GFCI protection, unless an assured equipment grounding conductor program is used.

w.1: The GFCI rule is for 120-V single-phase 15/20-A receptacles, not 480-V disconnects.
w.2: This charger is already on a GFCI outlet, so nothing more is required.
w.3: The rule targets temporary receptacles used by employees, not the permanent wiring.

mock1.q: A materials conveyor will be set up near an overhead distribution line that the utility confirms is 13.2 kV. What is the minimum clearance to maintain from the line?
o: 3 ft
6 ft
10 ft
50 ft
mock1.e: For lines rated 50 kV or less, the commonly required minimum clearance for equipment and unqualified workers is 10 ft. For cranes and derricks, 1926.1408 Table A gives 10 ft up to 50 kV. When the voltage is unknown, crane rules use 20 ft. The best practice is to have the utility de-energize or insulate the line.

w.0: 3 ft is far too close for an unqualified worker or equipment.
w.1: 6 ft is not the clearance for 13.2 kV lines.
w.3: 50 ft is more than required for this voltage, though larger clearances apply at very high voltages.

mock1.q: During a tear-off, a worker is exposed to 95 dBA for 4 hours and 100 dBA for 2 hours. Using OSHA's permissible times (95 dBA = 4 h, 100 dBA = 2 h), what is the noise dose, and is the exposure acceptable?
o: 0.75; within the limit
1.00; exactly at the limit
1.50; over the limit
2.00; over the limit
mock1.e: Dose = C1/T1 + C2/T2 = 4/4 + 2/2 = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.0. Any sum greater than 1.0 exceeds the permissible exposure, so controls and hearing protection are required.

w.0: 0.75 comes from using the wrong permissible times.
w.1: 1.00 counts only one of the two exposures.
w.2: 1.50 is an arithmetic error; each fraction equals 1.0.

mock1.q: A roofer will wear a tight-fitting half-face respirator while cutting fiber-cement panels. What must happen BEFORE the worker is fit-tested?
o: Three months of experience using respirators
A written test on the Hazard Communication standard
An annual physical exam including a chest X-ray
A medical evaluation determining the worker is able to use the respirator
mock1.e: Under the respiratory protection standard, the employer must provide a medical evaluation to determine the employee's ability to use a respirator before the employee is fit-tested or required to use it. Fit testing is then done before first use and at least annually.

w.0: No experience period is required; training is required.
w.1: HazCom training is separate and is not a prerequisite for fit testing.
w.2: A chest X-ray is not the prerequisite for respirator use.

mock1.q: A foreman wants to check the flash point of a solvent-based EPDM bonding adhesive. In which section of the 16-section Safety Data Sheet is it listed?
o: Section 2 — Hazard identification
Section 8 — Exposure controls/personal protection
Section 9 — Physical and chemical properties
Section 11 — Toxicological information
mock1.e: Section 9 lists physical and chemical properties, such as flash point, vapor pressure, and boiling point.

w.0: Section 2 lists the hazard classification, signal word, pictograms, and hazard statements.
w.1: Section 8 covers exposure limits, engineering controls, and PPE.
w.3: Section 11 covers health effects and toxicity data.

mock1.q: Two containers of roofing adhesive carry different signal words. Which signal word indicates the MORE severe hazard?
o: Danger
Caution
Notice
Warning
mock1.e: Under the GHS-aligned Hazard Communication Standard, "Danger" is used for the more severe hazard categories and "Warning" for the less severe.

w.1: "Caution" is not a GHS signal word.
w.2: "Notice" is a sign term for non-hazard information, not a label signal word.
w.3: "Warning" is the signal word for less severe hazards.

mock1.q: A 1970s built-up roof is to be torn off. Its black flashing cement and old felts are suspected of containing asbestos. What is the BEST first step?
o: Wet the roof thoroughly and proceed, because roofing asbestos is nonfriable
Re-cover the roof instead, so the asbestos never needs to be tested
Have the suspect materials sampled and analyzed before disturbing them
Use a power roof cutter with a dust bag to reduce the dust
mock1.e: Determine whether asbestos is present before disturbing it. If it is, removal is Class II work that requires specific methods (intact removal, wet methods, no dropping or throwing, isolating HVAC intakes) and a competent person. Environmental notification rules may also apply.

w.0: Wet methods are part of the procedure, but you can't pick the procedure until you know whether ACM is present. Nonfriable materials can become regulated when they are cut or abraded.
w.1: Re-covering is limited by code and doesn't remove the need to identify ACM that will be disturbed during the work.
w.3: Power cutting can release fibers. Cutting ACM roofing requires misting and specific controls.

mock1.src: 29 CFR 1926.1101(g)(8)(ii), (k); NRCA asbestos guide (paywalled; not read)

mock1.q: Asbestos-containing roofing material is being removed. Which practice is PROHIBITED?
o: Wrapping or bagging the material before lowering it
Keeping the roof-cutting machine blade continuously misted during use
Lowering the material to the ground through a covered, dust-tight chute
Dropping unwrapped removed material over the roof edge to the ground
mock1.e: Unwrapped or unbagged ACM roofing must be lowered by a covered, dust-tight chute, crane, or hoist, or it must be bagged or wrapped. It may never be dropped or thrown to the ground.

w.0: Bagging or wrapping is an approved method.
w.1: Continuous misting of cutting machines is required.
w.2: A dust-tight chute is an approved method.

mock1.q: The asphalt in a kettle ignites. What is the BEST immediate action?
o: Stir the asphalt so the burning surface is submerged
Close the kettle lid, shut off the burner, and use an appropriate extinguisher if needed
Add cold asphalt to lower the temperature quickly
Spray water into the kettle to cool the asphalt
mock1.e: Closing the lid smothers the fire by cutting off oxygen. Shutting off the fuel removes the heat source. A B-rated extinguisher can handle any remaining flame.

w.0: Stirring feeds oxygen and spreads the fire.
w.2: Adding material near an open fire exposes the worker and does not stop combustion.
w.3: Water on hot asphalt flashes to steam and sprays burning asphalt, making the fire far worse.

mock1.src: NRCA safety practice (NRCA Safety Manual — paywalled; not read); 29 CFR 1926.150

mock1.q: Under NRCA's CERTA (Certified Roofing Torch Applicator) program, how long must a fire watch continue after the last torch is turned off?
o: 30 minutes
1 hour
2 hours
Until the end of the shift only
mock1.e: CERTA requires a fire watch of at least 2 hours after torching ends, because smoldering fires in concealed spaces can take time to develop.

w.0: 30 minutes is too short under CERTA.
w.1: 1 hour appears in some fire codes, but CERTA requires 2 hours.
w.3: The shift may end sooner than 2 hours after torching; the watch is time-based.

mock1.src: NRCA CERTA Student Manual (public NRCA document)

mock1.q: Which temperature must hot roofing asphalt NEVER reach in the kettle?
o: Its softening point
Its flash point
Its equiviscous temperature (EVT)
mock1.e: Asphalt must never be heated to its flash point, where its vapors can ignite. Common practice keeps the kettle well below the flash point (often at least 25°F below). Application is done at the EVT ±25°F.

w.0: The softening point (roughly 135–225°F) is far below application temperature and is necessarily exceeded.
w.2: A fixed 350°F isn't the rule. Many asphalts are applied near or above 400°F, depending on their EVT.
w.3: EVT is the target application temperature, so it must be reached.

mock1.src: NRCA practice; asphalt bill of lading/SDS (flash point, EVT, FBT)

mock1.q: On a hot afternoon a roofer becomes confused, stops sweating, and has hot, dry skin. What is the most likely condition, and the correct response?
o: Heat exhaustion — let the worker rest in the truck until the shift ends
Heat stroke — call 911 and begin aggressive cooling immediately
Heat cramps — have the worker stretch and drink an electrolyte drink
Mild dehydration — give water and return him to work in 15 minutes
mock1.e: Confusion and hot, dry skin with little sweating are signs of heat stroke, a medical emergency. Call 911 and cool the worker aggressively (shade, ice or cold water, fanning) while waiting.

w.0: Heat exhaustion typically shows heavy sweating and cool, clammy skin. Leaving a confused worker alone in a hot truck is dangerous.
w.2: Heat cramps involve painful muscle spasms without confusion.
w.3: Returning a confused worker to the roof ignores a life-threatening emergency.

mock1.src: OSHA/NIOSH heat illness guidance; NRCA safety practice

mock1.q: A roofer falls, breaks a leg, and is admitted to the hospital overnight. How soon must the employer report the in-patient hospitalization to OSHA?
o: Within 8 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 7 days
Within 30 days
mock1.e: Work-related in-patient hospitalizations, amputations, and losses of an eye must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours. Fatalities must be reported within 8 hours.

w.0: 8 hours is the deadline for fatalities.
w.2: 7 calendar days is the deadline for entering a recordable case on the OSHA 300 log.
w.3: 30 days is not an OSHA reporting deadline.

mock1.q: Glass-fiber ply felts and modified-bitumen rolls are delivered to the site. How should they be stored?
o: On end (upright) on pallets off the ground, protected with breathable waterproof covers
On the roof deck mid-span between joists, to keep them close to the work
On the ground under the factory plastic wrap
Lying flat and stacked so the rolls don't roll away
mock1.e: NRCA practice is to store rolls on end to prevent flattening and deformation (which cause wrinkles and fishmouths), off the ground, and protected from moisture with breathable covers.

w.1: Concentrated loads belong over structural supports, not mid-span.
w.2: Factory wrap is for shipping, not weather protection. Rolls on the ground pick up moisture.
w.3: Rolls stored flat deform.

mock1.src: NRCA Roofing Manual practice (paywalled; not read); manufacturer storage instructions

mock1.q: Pallets of polyiso insulation will sit on the job for a week before use. What is the BEST protection?
o: Store them on the ground; the foil facers make the boards waterproof
Elevate the pallets and cover them with secured, breathable waterproof tarps
Leave the factory shrink-wrap on; it is designed for outdoor storage
Cover them tightly with black polyethylene sheet sealed to the ground
mock1.e: Insulation must be kept dry, off the ground, and covered with secured, breathable waterproof covers. Wet insulation loses R-value, its facers delaminate, and it can't be installed.

w.0: The facers don't protect the board edges, and ground contact wicks water in.
w.2: Factory wrap is not weather protection, and it often has openings or tears.
w.3: Non-breathable plastic sealed to the ground traps condensation under the cover.

mock1.src: NRCA practice; insulation manufacturer storage guidance

mock1.q: A homeowner wants new asphalt shingles installed over a roof that already has two layers of asphalt shingles. What is the best course of action?
o: Install the new layer if the owner signs a waiver
Install the new layer using longer nails
Tear off the existing layers to the deck; a third layer isn't permitted under the model codes
Install a new layer if the existing roof is dry
mock1.e: The model codes prohibit a new covering over an existing one when two or more applications already exist, when the existing roof is water-soaked or deteriorated, or when it is slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile. NRCA also generally favors tear-off.

w.0: An owner can't waive a code requirement.
w.1: Longer nails don't overcome the code prohibition.
w.3: Being dry doesn't matter when there are already two layers.

mock1.q: An infrared scan of a low-slope roof shows several warm areas after sunset. What is the BEST way to confirm whether the insulation in those areas is wet?
o: Take core cuts at the suspect areas and at a known-dry reference area
Walk the roof and feel for soft spots only
Wait for the next rain and look for leaks inside
Rescan the roof at noon the next day
mock1.e: Core cuts physically confirm the wetness and show the actual assembly. They are the standard verification for infrared, nuclear, and capacitance surveys. Patch each core immediately.

w.1: Soft spots can point to wet areas, but walking alone is unreliable and doesn't measure moisture.
w.2: Waiting for a leak lets damage continue and still doesn't locate the wet insulation.
w.3: Midday sun heats the whole surface and masks the differences infrared relies on. Scans are done after sunset.

mock1.src: NRCA practice (moisture surveys); ASTM C1153 (infrared imaging of roofs)

mock1.q: A new roof will go over a lightweight insulating concrete (LWIC) deck. How is the base sheet normally attached?
o: Loose-laid under the insulation with no attachment
Solid-mopped in hot asphalt to seal in the moisture
Adhered with solvent-based contact adhesive
Mechanically fastened with fasteners designed for LWIC, allowing moisture to vent
mock1.e: LWIC contains water that must be able to escape. Base sheets (often venting base sheets) are mechanically fastened with LWIC-specific fasteners, per the deck and roofing manufacturers.

w.0: An unattached base sheet provides no wind resistance or securement.
w.1: Solid mopping traps moisture and can cause blistering and poor adhesion.
w.2: Solvent contact adhesives are not the standard attachment to LWIC.

mock1.q: Which insulation board should NOT be set directly in hot asphalt?
o: Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
Perlite board
Polyisocyanurate
Wood fiberboard
mock1.e: Polystyrene (EPS and XPS) melts when it contacts hot asphalt, and solvents attack it. It needs a compatible cover board, or it has to be attached mechanically or with approved adhesives.

w.1: Perlite is compatible with hot asphalt and is often used as a cover board over foam.
w.2: Polyiso tolerates hot asphalt and is commonly set in it.
w.3: Fiberboard is compatible with hot asphalt.

mock1.q: A PVC membrane will be installed as a re-cover over an existing smooth-surfaced asphalt BUR. What is REQUIRED between them?
o: A separation layer or cover board approved by the PVC manufacturer
Nothing; PVC is chemically compatible with asphalt
A layer of hot asphalt to adhere the PVC directly
A coat of asphalt primer to improve adhesion
mock1.e: Asphalt and PVC are incompatible. Oils and plasticizers migrate, making the PVC brittle. A manufacturer-approved separation sheet or cover board is required.

w.1: PVC is not compatible with asphalt.
w.2: Adhering PVC directly in asphalt causes exactly the incompatibility problem.
w.3: Priming the asphalt doesn't separate it from the PVC.

mock1.q: A copper counterflashing drains onto a galvanized steel gutter. What is the most likely long-term result?
o: No reaction, because both metals are corrosion-resistant
Green staining on the gutter, with no loss of metal
Accelerated corrosion of the copper counterflashing
Accelerated corrosion of the galvanized gutter
mock1.e: Runoff carrying copper ions attacks zinc (galvanizing) and aluminum, which are less noble. The gutter corrodes.

w.0: The metals are dissimilar, and water provides the electrolyte.
w.1: Staining can occur, but the real concern is metal loss in the gutter.
w.2: Copper is the more noble metal and is protected in this pairing.

mock1.src: Galvanic series; NRCA architectural metal practice

mock1.q: Which ASTM D312 roofing asphalt has the HIGHEST softening point and is intended for the steepest slopes?
o: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV
mock1.e: Type IV ("special steep," about 210–225°F softening point) resists flow on steeper slopes and in hot climates. Type I (135–151°F) is the dead-level asphalt.

w.0: Type I has the lowest softening point and is for dead-level roofs.
w.1: Type II (158–176°F) is for low slopes.
w.2: Type III (185–205°F) is the most common BUR asphalt, but not the highest.

mock1.q: Hot asphalt will be applied directly to a clean, dry concrete deck. What should be applied first?
o: A coat of roof cement
ASTM D41 asphalt primer
A coal-tar pitch primer
Water, so the asphalt spreads more evenly
mock1.e: Asphalt primer (ASTM D41) penetrates the concrete surface and binds surface dust, so hot asphalt bonds properly. It is also used on metal surfaces.

w.0: Roof cement is a trowel-grade material, not a primer.
w.2: Coal-tar products are incompatible with asphalt systems.
w.3: Water must never be on a surface receiving hot asphalt; it causes steam blistering and poor bond.

mock1.q: For the same thickness, which roof insulation typically provides the HIGHEST R-value?
o: Perlite board
Mineral wool board
Expanded polystyrene (EPS)
Polyisocyanurate
mock1.e: Polyiso has the highest R per inch of common roof insulations (about 5.6–5.7 LTTR), though its performance drops in cold weather.

w.0: Perlite is roughly R-2.6 to 2.8 per inch.
w.1: Mineral wool is roughly R-3.7 to 4.2 per inch.
w.2: EPS is roughly R-3.6 to 4.2 per inch.

mock1.src: Manufacturer data (ASTM C1289, C578, C728, C726)

mock1.q: A heated Illinois office building requires a roof vapor retarder. Where should it be placed?
o: On the warm (interior) side of the insulation, below the insulation
Between two layers of insulation, at the midpoint
On top of the insulation, directly under the membrane
Anywhere, because location does not matter
mock1.e: A vapor retarder goes on the warm-in-winter side of the insulation. That keeps interior moisture from reaching surfaces colder than its dew point. In a heated building, that's below the insulation, on the deck side.

w.1: A midpoint location can leave the lower layer's cold face below the dew point, depending on the design.
w.2: A retarder under the membrane traps moisture inside the insulation, on the cold side.
w.3: Location is critical.

mock1.src: NRCA condensation guidance (paywalled; summary); building science practice

mock1.q: Which permeance defines a Class I vapor retarder?
o: 0.1 perm or less
More than 0.1 up to 1.0 perm
More than 1.0 up to 10 perm
More than 10 perm
mock1.e: Class I is 0.1 perm or less (e.g., polyethylene sheet, foil). Class II is more than 0.1 up to 1.0. Class III is more than 1.0 up to 10.

w.1: This range is Class II.
w.2: This range is Class III.
w.3: Above 10 perms, a material is considered vapor-permeable.

mock1.q: A gable roof has a plan area (including overhangs) of 48 ft × 32 ft and an 8:12 slope (slope factor 1.202). Add 10% waste and round up to whole squares before converting to bundles. At 3 bundles per square, how many bundles are needed?
mock1.e: Plan area = 48 × 32 = 1,536 sq ft. Roof area = 1,536 × 1.202 = 1,846.3 sq ft. Add 10% → 2,030.9 sq ft = 20.31 squares → round up to 21 squares. 21 × 3 = 63 bundles.

w.0: 57 bundles (19 squares) ignores the 10% waste.
w.1: 60 bundles (20 squares) rounds down instead of up.
w.3: 66 bundles (22 squares) over-rounds or adds extra waste.

mock1.q: Standard 12 × 36 in three-tab shingles at a 5-in exposure are installed with 6 nails each for high wind. How many nails are needed per square?
mock1.e: Shingles per square = 14,400 sq in ÷ (5 in × 36 in) = 80. 80 × 6 nails = 480 nails.

w.0: 320 is the count at 4 nails per shingle.
w.1: 400 corresponds to 5 nails per shingle.
w.3: 540 would require 90 shingles per square, which is the wrong exposure math.

mock1.src: Standard estimating method; manufacturer high-wind fastening

mock1.q: A 6:12 hip roof has a common-rafter run of 14 ft. Using a hip/valley length factor of 1.5 for 6:12, how long is each hip (excluding overhang)?
mock1.e: Hip length = common run × hip factor = 14 × 1.5 = 21.0 ft. For 6:12, the factor is √(6² + 288)/12 = 18/12 = 1.5.

w.0: 15.7 ft is the common-rafter length (14 × 1.118), not the hip.
w.1: 18.0 ft misapplies the factor.
w.2: 19.8 ft is 14 × √2, which ignores the rise.

mock1.src: Roof framing geometry; standard estimating method

mock1.q: During tear-off, the crew finds a 3 ft × 3 ft area of steel deck that is rusted through. What should the roofing contractor do?
o: Cover the hole with a piece of plywood and continue
Continue roofing; structural issues are not the roofer's concern
Fill the area with extra insulation layers so the membrane is supported
Stop work in that area, document the condition, and notify the owner or GC in writing so the deck can be repaired before it is roofed over
mock1.e: The roofer does not design or certify the structure but must not roof over an unsuitable deck. The best practice is to stop, document, and notify in writing, then proceed after an authorized repair (often a unit-price item).

w.0: An unauthorized plywood patch is not an engineered steel deck repair and may not carry loads or hold fasteners.
w.1: The roofer is expected to verify that the deck is suitable to receive roofing.
w.2: Insulation doesn't restore structural capacity.

mock1.src: NRCA practice (deck suitability); standard specification language [INFERENCE]

mock1.q: A new ACQ pressure-treated wood nailer will be in direct contact with an aluminum drip edge. What is the concern, and how is it addressed?
o: The copper-based treatment corrodes the aluminum; separate them or use a compatible metal
The aluminum rots the wood; seal the wood with roof cement
There is no concern, because treated wood is inert
The nailer will shrink; use longer fasteners
mock1.e: Copper-based treatments such as ACQ and CA are corrosive to aluminum and to light galvanizing. Isolate them with a separation membrane, or use compatible metals and fasteners (hot-dip galvanized or stainless).

w.1: Aluminum does not rot wood.
w.2: Modern copper-based treatments are chemically active.
w.3: Shrinkage is not the compatibility issue this question describes.

mock1.src: Treated-wood and fastener manufacturer guidance; IRC R317.3 [JURISDICTION]

mock1.q: Condensation will form on the underside of a roof deck when the deck's surface temperature is:
o: Equal to the outdoor air temperature
Above the interior air temperature
Above the dew point of the interior air
Below the dew point of the interior air that reaches it
mock1.e: Water vapor condenses on any surface colder than the dew point of the air touching it. Controlling air leakage and vapor keeps moist interior air from reaching cold surfaces.

w.0: Outdoor temperature alone doesn't decide it. What matters is the surface temperature compared with the dew point of the air reaching it.
w.1: A surface warmer than the air can't collect condensation from that air.
w.2: Above the dew point, there is no condensation.

mock1.q: Pallets of shingle bundles are being loaded onto a wood-framed roof with a boom truck. What is the BEST practice?
o: Distribute the bundles in small stacks near the ridge or over bearing walls, rather than landing full pallets mid-span
Put the pallets wherever the boom reaches, since the roof is designed for any construction load
Land full pallets in the center of the roof to shorten carrying distances
Stack all bundles at the eave so they are ready to install
mock1.e: A full pallet can put about 200 psf on a small area, far more than typical roof design loads. Spreading bundles near bearing points, and straddling the ridge where the manufacturer allows, protects the structure and keeps the load balanced.

w.1: Roofs are not designed for unlimited concentrated construction loads.
w.2: Concentrated mid-span loads can overload the rafters or trusses.
w.3: Stacking at the eave concentrates the load on the overhang and creates a falling-object hazard at the edge.

mock1.src: NRCA material handling practice; manufacturer loading guidance

mock1.q: What is the minimum roof slope for asphalt shingles under the model codes and NRCA practice?
mock1.e: Asphalt shingles may be installed on slopes of 2:12 or greater. Slopes from 2:12 up to less than 4:12 need special (double) underlayment.

w.0: 1:12 is the minimum for mineral-surfaced roll roofing, not shingles.
w.2: 3:12 is the minimum for wood shingles, wood shakes, and metal shingles.
w.3: 4:12 is where normal single-layer underlayment applies, and it is the slate minimum.

mock1.q: Asphalt shingles are being installed on a 3:12 roof. How should the felt underlayment be applied (no self-adhered membrane used)?
o: No underlayment is needed under laminated shingles
One layer lapped 2 in at the head laps
One layer lapped 6 in at the head laps
Two layers: a 19-in starter strip at the eave, then 36-in sheets lapped 19 in
mock1.e: For slopes from 2:12 up to less than 4:12, double coverage is required. Begin with a 19-in-wide strip at the eave, then lap each 36-in sheet 19 in over the previous one, so every point has two layers.

w.0: Underlayment is required regardless of shingle type.
w.1: A single layer with 2-in laps is the method for 4:12 and steeper.
w.2: A single layer with a wider lap is still only one layer in most places.

mock1.q: Which sequence is correct at the EAVE of an asphalt shingle roof, following the model-code method?
o: Deck → drip edge → shingles → underlayment
Deck → drip edge → underlayment over the drip edge flange → starter strip → shingles
Deck → underlayment → drip edge over the underlayment → starter strip → shingles
Deck → starter strip → drip edge → underlayment → shingles
mock1.e: At the eave, the drip edge goes on the deck first and the underlayment laps over its flange. Water running down the underlayment then lands on the metal and drips clear.

w.0: Underlayment goes under the shingles, never over them.
w.2: This is the sequence for the RAKE, not the eave. At the eave it lets water get behind the flange.
w.3: The starter strip goes on top of the underlayment and drip edge.

mock1.q: At the RAKE edge, how does the drip edge relate to the underlayment?
o: The drip edge is installed over the underlayment
The drip edge is installed under the underlayment
The drip edge is installed over the shingles
No drip edge is used at rakes
mock1.e: At rakes, the underlayment is installed first and the drip edge laps over it. That keeps wind-driven rain from getting under the underlayment edge.

w.1: Drip edge under the underlayment is the EAVE method.
w.2: Shingles overlap the drip edge; the metal is never placed on top of them.
w.3: Code and manufacturers call for drip edge at both eaves and rakes.

mock1.q: Where an ice barrier is required under the model code, how far up the roof must it extend?
o: From the eave edge to a point 12 in beyond the fascia
From the eave edge to a point at least 24 in inside the exterior wall line of the building
Only over the overhang, to the face of the exterior wall
36 in up the roof, measured along the slope, regardless of overhang
mock1.e: The ice barrier (two layers of underlayment cemented together, or a self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen sheet) extends from the lowest edges of all roof surfaces to a point at least 24 in inside the exterior wall line.

w.0: Stopping 12 in past the fascia leaves the area over the heated space unprotected.
w.2: Ice dams back water up over the heated space, beyond the wall line.
w.3: A fixed 36-in width may fall short on wide overhangs or steep slopes.

mock1.q: A 7:12 roof (slope factor 1.158) has an 18-in horizontal overhang. The ice barrier must extend 24 in horizontally inside the exterior wall line. What is the minimum ice-barrier width measured along the slope from the eave edge?
mock1.e: Horizontal distance = 18 + 24 = 42 in. Along the slope: 42 × 1.158 = 48.6 in. A single 36-in-wide ice-barrier course is not enough; you need two courses.

w.0: 42.0 in is the horizontal distance, not measured along the slope.
w.1: 44.4 in uses the wrong slope factor.
w.3: 52.0 in adds extra width that isn't required.

mock1.q: After a moderate windstorm, rows of laminated shingles installed last fall have blown off. Nail holes are visible above the sealant line of the underlying course. What is the most likely cause?
o: Using starter strips at the eave
High nailing — fasteners above the nailing zone missed the underlying course
Shingles from the same production lot
Inadequate attic ventilation
mock1.e: When nails are placed above the manufacturer's nailing zone, they don't pass through the shingle below, so each shingle has half the intended holding power. Combined with sealant strips that haven't sealed (common with fall installation), this is the classic cause of blow-offs.

w.0: Starter strips improve wind resistance at the eave.
w.2: Using one production lot prevents color shading and doesn't affect wind resistance.
w.3: Poor ventilation causes curling and premature aging, not rows of blow-offs with high nail holes.

mock1.q: Nail heads are pushing up under the shingles in several spots about a year after installation. Which installation error most commonly causes this?
o: Using galvanized nails
Underdriven nails, or deck movement from wet or unsupported sheathing
Overdriven nails that cut through the shingle mat
Too many nails per shingle
mock1.e: Underdriven nails, or nails backing out of a deck that shrinks and moves, lift the shingle above. That prevents sealing and eventually tears the shingle.

w.0: Galvanized nails are the standard corrosion-resistant fastener.
w.2: Overdriven nails cause cut-through and blow-offs, not raised heads.
w.3: The fastener count doesn't cause pops.

mock1.q: For a standard installation under the model code (not high-wind), what is the minimum number of fasteners per asphalt strip shingle?
mock1.e: The code minimum is 4 fasteners per strip shingle (2 per individual shingle). Manufacturers typically require 6 for high-wind areas and very steep slopes.

w.0: Two fasteners is the minimum for individual (not strip) shingles.
w.1: Three is not a code or manufacturer standard.
w.3: Six is the high-wind/steep-slope requirement, not the standard minimum.

mock1.q: Laminated shingles are being installed on a mansard with a 24:12 slope. Beyond the standard application, what do manufacturers typically require?
o: Four nails per shingle placed higher on the shingle
No special requirements; steep slopes shed water faster
Six nails per shingle and hand-sealing each shingle with asphalt roof cement
Two layers of underlayment lapped 19 in
mock1.e: Above about 21:12, sealant strips alone may not hold because gravity pulls the shingles away. Manufacturers call for extra nails (typically 6) and hand-sealing with spots of roof cement.

w.0: Higher nailing reduces holding power; nails must stay in the nailing zone.
w.1: Very steep slopes need special fastening.
w.3: Double underlayment is the rule for LOW slopes (2:12 to below 4:12).

mock1.q: Shingles are installed in December at 30°F, and a windy week is forecast. What should the crew do to protect the new roof?
o: Add extra nails above the nailing zone
Nothing, because sealant strips activate in any temperature
Cover the entire roof with plastic sheeting until spring
Hand-seal the shingles with asphalt roof cement per the manufacturer, since the sealant strips won't activate until warm weather
mock1.e: Sealant strips need heat from the sun to bond. In cold weather, the shingles stay unsealed and vulnerable to wind until they seal. Hand-sealing gives immediate resistance.

w.0: Nails above the nailing zone miss the underlying course and reduce holding power.
w.1: Sealant strips are heat-activated.
w.2: Covering the roof with plastic is not a practical or recommended method.

mock1.q: Which valley method do manufacturers generally NOT recommend for laminated (architectural) shingles?
o: Open valley with a metal liner and cut shingle edges set in cement
Open metal (W-profile) valley
Closed-cut valley
Woven valley
mock1.e: Laminated shingles are thick and stiff and don't bend smoothly through a woven valley. The result is bridging and voids. Closed-cut or open valleys are used instead.

w.0: This is an open metal valley, which is appropriate.
w.1: An open metal valley is appropriate for any shingle type.
w.2: Closed-cut is the most common valley for laminated shingles.

mock1.q: A closed-cut valley joins a 4:12 porch roof and a 10:12 main roof. What is the recommended sequence?
o: Run the shingles from the 10:12 plane across the valley first, then cut the 4:12 plane's shingles
Weave both planes through the valley
Cut both planes back 2 in from the centerline to form an open valley
Run the shingles from the 4:12 plane across the valley first, then cut the 10:12 plane's shingles back from the valley centerline
mock1.e: Manufacturers generally have the lower-slope (or smaller) plane's shingles run across the valley first. The steeper plane's faster-flowing water then runs over the cut edge, not into it.

w.0: That reverses the recommended order and sends the steeper plane's water against the cut edge.
w.1: Weaving is a different valley method and isn't recommended for laminated shingles.
w.2: Cutting both sides makes an open valley, which needs a metal or roll-roofing liner.

mock1.q: In a closed-cut valley, how are the cut-side shingles finished?
o: Cut about 2 in back from the valley centerline, clip the upper corner at 45°, embed the edge in asphalt cement, and keep nails at least about 6 in from the centerline
Leave the shingles uncut and fold them up the other plane
Cut exactly on the centerline, with nails driven through the valley center to hold the edge
Cut 6 in back from the centerline, with no cement
mock1.e: The cut side is trimmed about 2 in back from the centerline. The upper corner is clipped so water isn't directed under the shingle, and the edge is set in cement. No fasteners go within about 6 in of the centerline, where the most water flows.

w.1: Folding the shingles doesn't create a closed-cut valley.
w.2: Nails in the valley center are a classic cause of valley leaks.
w.3: 6 in is the distance to keep nails from the centerline, not the cut line, and the cement is part of the method.

mock1.q: Under the model code, what is the minimum width of a metal valley lining for an open valley with asphalt shingles?
o: 12 in
16 in
24 in
36 in
mock1.e: The model code table for valley linings requires metal valley flashing at least 24 in wide.

w.0: 12 in is too narrow to carry the valley's water.
w.1: 16 in is too narrow for code metal valley linings.
w.3: 36 in is the common width for the valley UNDERLAYMENT, not the metal lining.

mock1.q: How should each piece of step flashing be fastened where a shingle roof meets a sidewall?
o: Fasteners through both legs so the piece can't move
One fastener through the wall leg into the wall framing
Sealant only, with no fasteners
One fastener in the roof leg near the top edge, into the deck; the wall leg is not nailed
mock1.e: Fastening the roof leg only, near the top where the next shingle covers it, lets the roof and wall move independently. The fastener stays covered, and the vertical leg stays free.

w.0: Nailing both legs locks the flashing and invites cracking and leaks.
w.1: Nailing the wall leg ties the flashing to the wall and can tear it as the structures move.
w.2: Sealant alone isn't a reliable attachment.

mock1.src: NRCA steep-slope flashing practice; manufacturer instructions

mock1.q: A new shingle roof leaks along a sidewall. The installer used one continuous L-shaped flashing along the wall instead of step flashing. Why does this leak?
o: Continuous flashing always causes condensation
The flashing color attracted too much heat
Water running down the vertical leg and along the flashing gets into the shingle laps, because the flashing isn't interleaved with each course
The continuous flashing was too thick
mock1.e: Step flashing is woven into each course, so each piece sheds water onto the shingle below it. A continuous L-flashing carries water along its length and dumps it under the shingle laps.

w.0: Condensation is unrelated to this flashing error.
w.1: Heat is irrelevant here.
w.3: Thickness is not the issue.

mock1.q: The wall sheathing below the lower end of a roof-to-wall intersection is rotting where the eave meets a two-story wall. What missing component most likely caused this?
o: Ice barrier at the rake
A kickout (diverter) flashing at the bottom of the step flashing
A cricket at the chimney
A ridge vent
mock1.e: Where a roof-wall intersection ends before the wall does, a kickout flashing diverts water off the wall and into the gutter. Without it, water runs behind the cladding and rots the wall.

w.0: Ice barrier at the rake doesn't address water at the bottom of a sidewall.
w.2: Crickets divert water around chimneys and wide penetrations, not at sidewall eaves.
w.3: A ridge vent doesn't affect water at a sidewall-eave intersection.

mock1.q: A chimney measures 36 in across, perpendicular to the slope, on a 6:12 roof. What is required on its upslope side?
o: Only step flashing
A cricket (saddle)
A continuous bead of sealant
A pitch pan
mock1.e: A cricket or saddle is required on the ridge side of any chimney or penetration more than 30 in wide, measured perpendicular to the slope. It diverts water and debris around the chimney.

w.0: Step flashing alone leaves a dam where water and debris collect behind the chimney.
w.2: Sealant is not a substitute for a cricket.
w.3: Pitch pans are low-slope membrane details, and a last resort even there.

mock1.q: Why is chimney flashing made of two parts, a base (step) flashing and a counterflashing set into the mortar joints?
o: The roof and the chimney move independently; each part is attached to only one of them, and the counterflashing laps over the base flashing
The counterflashing holds the shingles down in the wind
Two layers of metal are always required by code for fire resistance
The base flashing supports the chimney's weight
mock1.e: The chimney and the roof framing move differently through settlement, thermal movement, and shrinkage. The base flashing is fastened to the roof, and the counterflashing to the masonry. The lap lets them slide without tearing.

w.1: The counterflashing does not hold shingles.
w.2: Fire resistance is not the reason for the two-part system.
w.3: Flashing carries no structural load.

mock1.q: How should the flange of a plumbing vent flashing be integrated with the shingles?
o: The flange goes under the underlayment
The upper part of the flange goes under the shingles above; the lower part lies on top of the shingles below
The whole flange goes on top of the shingles, sealed with cement
The whole flange goes under the shingles
mock1.e: Following the water-shedding rule, water coming down the roof flows over the shingles above and onto the flange, then off the flange onto the shingles below. It never flows under a lap.

w.0: The flange must integrate with the shingles, not sit under the underlayment.
w.2: A flange fully on top lets water run under its upper edge.
w.3: A flange fully under the shingles traps water at its lower edge and directs it under the courses below.

mock1.q: An attic has a new ridge vent, the original gable-end louvers, and a powered attic fan. The homeowner reports wind-driven snow entering at the ridge vent. What is the BEST recommendation?
o: Use a single exhaust type with adequate soffit intake — for example, keep the ridge vent and remove or block the gable louvers and the powered fan
Add a second powered fan
Add more gable louvers
Seal all soffit vents to stop drafts
mock1.e: Different exhaust vents in one attic short-circuit each other. The fan or a gable vent can pull air in through the ridge vent, drawing in snow and rain. Balanced soffit intake with one exhaust type is recommended.

w.1: A second fan worsens the short-circuiting.
w.2: More gable louvers add to the short-circuiting.
w.3: Sealing the soffits removes the intake and makes the exhaust vents pull air (and weather) in through the ridge.

mock1.src: Shingle and ventilation manufacturer guidance; NRCA ventilation practice

mock1.q: An attic floor measures 2,100 sq ft. Using the 1/300 ratio with half the net free area at the ridge, how many linear feet of ridge vent rated at 18 sq in of net free area per foot are needed?
o: 14 ft
24 ft
28 ft
56 ft
mock1.e: Required NFA = 2,100 ÷ 300 = 7 sq ft = 1,008 sq in. Half is exhaust: 504 sq in. 504 ÷ 18 = 28 linear feet.

w.0: 14 ft is half the correct number, from splitting the exhaust twice.
w.1: 24 ft comes from a different attic area.
w.3: 56 ft puts all of the required NFA at the ridge.

mock1.q: A house has recurring ice dams and interior leaks at the eaves every winter. What is the BEST long-term correction?
o: Install a second layer of shingles at the eaves
Install heavier shingles at the eaves
Remove the gutters
Air-seal and insulate the attic floor and ensure balanced ventilation, so the roof deck stays cold
mock1.e: Ice dams form when heat leaking into the attic melts snow, and the meltwater refreezes at the cold eave. Air sealing, insulation, and ventilation prevent the dam. An ice barrier reduces damage but doesn't stop dams from forming.

w.0: Extra shingle layers don't stop the dam, and re-cover limits may apply.
w.1: Shingle weight doesn't change the heat loss that causes the dam.
w.2: Removing gutters doesn't address the cause.

mock1.src: NRCA condensation/ventilation guidance; building science practice

mock1.q: Concrete tile is proposed for a 3:12 roof. Under the model code, is it permitted?
o: Yes, because the minimum is 2½:12, but slopes from 2½:12 up to below 4:12 require double underlayment
Yes, with a single layer of underlayment
No, because the minimum slope for tile is 4:12
No, because tile requires at least 6:12
mock1.e: Clay and concrete tile require a minimum slope of 2½:12. Between 2½:12 and 4:12, the code requires double underlayment.

w.1: A single underlayment layer is for 4:12 and steeper.
w.2: 4:12 is the minimum for slate, not tile.
w.3: 6:12 is not the tile minimum.

mock1.q: An owner wants to replace an asphalt shingle roof with concrete tile. What should be verified FIRST?
o: That the tile color matches the neighborhood
That the roof structure can carry the added weight of tile
That the attic has a ridge vent
That the gutters are large enough
mock1.e: Concrete and clay tile weigh several times more than asphalt shingles (often about 9–12 psf versus about 2–4 psf). The structure must be evaluated before the conversion.

w.0: Aesthetics are secondary to structural adequacy.
w.2: Ventilation is secondary to structure for this decision.
w.3: Gutter size is a secondary concern.

mock1.q: 24-in-long slates are installed with a 3-in headlap. What is the exposure?
o: 9.0 in
mock1.e: Slate exposure = (length − headlap) ÷ 2 = (24 − 3) ÷ 2 = 10.5 in.

w.0: 9.0 in subtracts too much.
w.2: 12.0 in is half the length, which ignores the headlap.
w.3: 21.0 in forgets to divide by 2. Each course must be covered by the two courses above it.

mock1.src: NRCA slate practice (Steep-slope manual — paywalled); standard slate formula

mock1.q: Which fastening practice is correct for slate?
o: Roofing staples at the head of each slate
Two copper (or stainless) nails per slate, driven so the slate hangs on the nails, not drawn tight
One nail at the center of the slate
Two electro-galvanized nails driven tight
mock1.e: Slate lasts for generations and needs fasteners that last as long, such as copper or stainless steel. Driving nails tight cracks the slate. It should hang on the nails.

w.0: Staples are not used for slate.
w.2: Slate requires two nails.
w.3: Electro-galvanized nails corrode long before the slate wears out, and tight nailing cracks slate.

mock1.src: NRCA slate practice; slate industry guidance

mock1.q: Under ASTM C406, what service life is expected for a Grade S1 roofing slate?
o: 20–40 years
40–75 years
More than 75 years
10–20 years
mock1.e: ASTM C406 grades roofing slate as S1 (service life over 75 years), S2 (40–75), and S3 (20–40).

w.0: 20–40 years is Grade S3.
w.1: 40–75 years is Grade S2.
w.3: 10–20 years is not an ASTM C406 grade.

mock1.q: Wood shakes are being installed over spaced sheathing. What is placed between the courses?
o: An 18-in-wide strip of No. 30 felt interlayment in each course
A 6-in strip of aluminum foil
Nothing, because shakes are self-sealing
A full self-adhered membrane under every course
mock1.e: Shakes are split and irregular, so they need an 18-in-wide No. 30 felt interlayment between courses. It is positioned above the butt a distance of twice the exposure, to block wind-driven rain.

w.1: Foil is not the specified interlayment.
w.2: Shakes are not self-sealing; the interlayment is required.
w.3: A full self-adhered membrane under each course would trap moisture and isn't the standard method.

mock1.src: IRC R905.8.7 [JURISDICTION]; Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau practice

mock1.q: What spacing is recommended between adjacent sawn wood shingles in the same course?
o: No gap (butted tight)
¼ to ⅜ in
⅜ to ⅝ in
1 to 1½ in
mock1.e: Wood shingles are spaced ¼ to ⅜ in apart to allow for swelling when wet. Shakes use ⅜ to ⅝ in.

w.0: Tight shingles buckle when they swell.
w.2: ⅜ to ⅝ in is the spacing for shakes.
w.3: 1 to 1½ in is too wide. 1½ in is the minimum side-joint OFFSET between courses.

mock1.q: What is the model-code minimum slope for lapped, non-soldered metal roof panels installed WITHOUT applied lap sealant?
mock1.e: Lapped, non-soldered seam metal panels without lap sealant need at least 3:12. With applied lap sealant, the minimum is ½:12. Standing-seam panels can go down to ¼:12.

w.0: ¼:12 is the standing-seam minimum.
w.1: ½:12 applies when lap sealant is used.
w.3: 4:12 is not the metal-panel threshold.

mock1.q: A 30-ft copper panel sees a 120°F temperature swing. Copper's coefficient is 9.4 × 10⁻⁶ in/in/°F. How much does the panel expand and contract?
mock1.e: ΔL = α × L × ΔT = 9.4 × 10⁻⁶ × 360 in × 120°F = 0.406 in, or about 0.41 in. Details and clips must accommodate this movement.

w.0: 0.28 in uses the steel coefficient (6.5 × 10⁻⁶), which gives 0.281 in.
w.2: 0.55 in comes from using the wrong length or temperature swing.
w.3: 0.81 in is double the correct value.

mock1.src: Thermal expansion formula; published coefficients of expansion

mock1.q: What is the preferred way to cut prefinished (painted) steel roof panels on the job?
o: Shears, nibblers, or a cutting tool that doesn't throw hot particles
A torch
Any saw, as long as the crew wears eye protection
An abrasive cut-off wheel on a grinder
mock1.e: Abrasive cutting throws hot metal particles that burn the paint and zinc coating and embed in nearby panels, where they rust. Shears and nibblers cut cleanly without heat. Clean up the swarf the same day.

w.1: A torch destroys the coating and the panel edge.
w.2: PPE protects the worker, not the panel.
w.3: Abrasive wheels damage the coating and cause rust staining.

mock1.src: Metal panel manufacturer instructions; NRCA metal practice

mock1.q: On a clay or concrete tile roof, which layer serves as the primary long-term waterproofing?
o: The underlayment beneath the tile
The battens
The mortar at the ridge
The tile itself
mock1.e: Tile sheds most water, but wind-driven rain and snow get past it. The underlayment is the true waterproofing layer, so it must be durable, correctly lapped, and properly flashed.

w.1: Battens hold the tile; they don't waterproof anything.
w.2: Ridge mortar only secures and closes the ridge.
w.3: Tile is water-shedding, not watertight.

mock1.src: Tile industry and NRCA tile practice

mock1.q: What minimum slope do the model building codes require for single-ply and modified-bitumen roof membranes, and what does NRCA recommend designing for?
o: ⅛ in per ft
¼ in per ft
½ in per ft
1 in per ft
mock1.e: Most membrane systems require a minimum slope of ¼:12 (2%) for positive drainage. Coal-tar BUR is the exception, with a ⅛:12 minimum.

w.0: ⅛:12 applies to coal-tar built-up roofs only.
w.2: ½:12 is more than the minimum.
w.3: 1:12 is more than the minimum.

mock1.q: Under NRCA's widely cited definition, water is considered "ponding" when it remains on a roof for how long after a rain, under conditions that allow drying?
o: 12 hours
24 hours
48 hours
7 days
mock1.e: NRCA defines ponding as water that remains on the roof surface 48 hours after the end of a rain, under conditions conducive to drying.

w.0: 12 hours is too short.
w.1: 24 hours is not the NRCA benchmark.
w.3: 7 days is not the definition.

mock1.q: How are field seams in a modern EPDM roof normally made?
o: Clean and prime both surfaces, let the primer flash off, apply seam tape, and roll it
Hot-air weld the overlap
Torch the lap until bitumen bleeds out
Mop the lap with hot asphalt
mock1.e: EPDM is a thermoset rubber, so it can't be re-melted or welded. Seams use primer and factory seam tape, rolled with a silicone roller.

w.1: Hot-air welding is for thermoplastics (TPO, PVC).
w.2: Torching is for modified bitumen.
w.3: Asphalt is incompatible with EPDM.

mock1.src: EPDM manufacturer instructions; NRCA Membrane practice

mock1.q: A fully adhered EPDM system uses solvent-based bonding (contact) adhesive. What is the correct procedure?
o: Apply adhesive to the substrate only and immediately lay the wet membrane into it
Apply adhesive to both the membrane underside and the substrate, let it flash until tacky, then mate them and broom or roll
Apply adhesive to the membrane only
Apply adhesive in beads 12 in apart, like insulation adhesive
mock1.e: Contact adhesives work by coating both surfaces and letting the solvent flash off until the adhesive is tacky but won't string. Then the surfaces are mated.

w.0: A wet, one-sided application traps solvent and bonds poorly (blistering).
w.2: One side only is not how contact adhesive works.
w.3: Bead application is for low-rise foam insulation adhesive, not EPDM bonding adhesive.

mock1.q: A crew performs a test weld on TPO and peels the sample apart by hand. Which result indicates a GOOD weld?
o: The two sheets separate cleanly along the weld interface
The weld is ½ in wide
The membrane surface is brown and glossy along the seam
The membrane tears or delaminates outside the weld (the sheet fails, not the seam)
mock1.e: In a properly fused thermoplastic seam, the weld is stronger than the membrane. The peel sample fails in the membrane (film tearing or exposed scrim), not at the interface.

w.0: Clean separation at the interface is a cold (unfused) weld.
w.1: Weld width must meet the manufacturer's minimum, commonly about 1½ in; ½ in is too narrow.
w.2: Browning and scorching suggest a burnt weld from too much heat.

mock1.src: TPO manufacturer welding instructions; NRCA practice

mock1.q: When should thermoplastic seam test welds be made?
o: Only when a seam fails inspection
Once a week
At the start of each day and whenever conditions change (temperature, wind, humidity, power source, or welder settings)
Once, when the welder is first purchased
mock1.e: Welding parameters depend on ambient and membrane conditions. Test welds at the start of the day and after any change keep the welder settings right.

w.0: Testing only after a failure is reactive and lets bad seams get installed.
w.1: Weekly testing misses daily condition changes.
w.3: Conditions change daily, so a one-time test isn't enough.

mock1.q: Six months after installation, a built-up roof has several soft, domed blisters between the plies. What is the most likely cause?
o: Too much aggregate
Using Type III asphalt
Voids with trapped air or moisture between plies, from incomplete mopping or wet felts
Too steep a slope
mock1.e: BUR blisters form where air or moisture is trapped in voids between plies. Sun heat expands it and lifts the plies. Complete moppings, brooming, and dry materials prevent them.

w.0: Aggregate protects the roof and doesn't cause interply blisters.
w.1: Type III is the most common BUR asphalt.
w.3: Slope is linked to slippage, not blistering.

mock1.src: NRCA Membrane manual practice (paywalled); Repair Manual (paywalled)

mock1.q: On a 1:12 built-up roof, the plies have slid downslope and exposed the laps at the top edge. What are the most likely causes?
o: Insulation that was too thick
A flood coat that was too thin
Too few plies
Asphalt with too low a softening point, excessive interply asphalt, and no backnailing
mock1.e: Slippage happens when interply asphalt softens and flows. Causes include too low a softening point (the wrong asphalt type), too much asphalt, overheating (which lowers the softening point), and a lack of mechanical backnailing on steeper slopes.

w.0: Insulation thickness doesn't cause slippage.
w.1: A thin flood coat causes aggregate loss, not ply slippage.
w.2: The ply count doesn't cause slippage.

mock1.q: For which roof systems are 45° cant strips normally installed at the base of walls and curbs?
o: Asphalt shingle systems
TPO and PVC systems
EPDM systems
Built-up and modified-bitumen systems
mock1.e: Bituminous plies and flashings crack if bent at a sharp 90° angle, so cants provide a gradual transition. Single-ply membranes are flexible enough to turn 90° without a cant.

w.0: Shingle sidewalls use step flashing, not cant strips.
w.1: TPO and PVC do not need cant strips.
w.2: EPDM does not need cant strips.

mock1.q: What minimum base flashing height, above the finished roof surface, does NRCA recommend at walls and curbs?
o: 4 in
6 in
8 in
12 in
mock1.e: NRCA recommends base flashings at least 8 in above the finished roof surface, to stay above ponding, snow, and splash.

w.0: 4 in is the typical counterflashing lap, not the base flashing height.
w.1: 6 in is below NRCA's recommendation.
w.3: 12 in exceeds the minimum.

mock1.q: A rooftop has an irregular steel angle penetration. Which statement about pitch pans is MOST accurate?
o: They are a last resort, and the pourable sealer must be crowned to shed water and maintained regularly
They are the preferred flashing for all round pipes
They require no maintenance once filled
They should be filled with water-based roof coating
mock1.e: Pitch pans depend on sealant, which shrinks and separates over time. NRCA considers them a last resort, used only when a curb or a prefabricated boot can't be used. Fill them with pourable sealer crowned to shed water, and inspect them regularly.

w.1: Round pipes are better flashed with prefabricated boots or flanged collars.
w.2: Pitch pans need ongoing maintenance.
w.3: Coatings are not pourable sealers and won't fill a pan properly.

mock1.src: NRCA Membrane manual details (paywalled; widely published)

mock1.q: What is the typical application method for APP (atactic polypropylene) modified bitumen?
o: Torch-applied (heat-welded)
Hot-air welded, like TPO
Ballasted, like EPDM
Hot-mopped with Type I asphalt
mock1.e: APP is a plastomeric modifier, and APP sheets are typically torch-applied. Some cold-applied APP products exist. SBS sheets are commonly hot-mopped, cold-applied, self-adhered, or torched.

w.1: Hot-air welding is a thermoplastic single-ply method.
w.2: Mod-bit is adhered or torched, not ballasted.
w.3: APP is generally not hot-mopped. Hot mopping is typical of SBS.

mock1.q: What does a uniform bleed-out of about ¼ to ½ in along a torch-applied mod-bit lap indicate?
o: The sheet was overheated and must be removed
Too little heat was used
The lap has a void underneath
The bitumen was heated enough to flow and fuse the lap
mock1.e: A consistent small bleed-out shows the bitumen reached flowing temperature and fused across the lap. No bleed-out suggests an unfused lap. Excessive bleed-out suggests overheating.

w.0: Overheating shows as excessive bleed-out and scorching, not a uniform ¼–½ in.
w.1: Too little heat shows as no bleed-out.
w.2: Voids are indicated by a missing bleed-out.

mock1.q: A restaurant's kitchen exhaust fan discharges grease onto the roof. Which membrane is generally the most resistant to grease and animal fats?
o: Smooth-surfaced asphalt BUR
Unprotected SBS mod-bit
EPDM
PVC (specifically a grease-resistant formulation)
mock1.e: PVC membranes, especially grease- and chemical-resistant formulations, resist fats and oils better than EPDM and asphaltic membranes. Grease containment at the fan is still recommended.

w.0: Asphalt is softened by oils and greases.
w.1: Asphaltic mod-bit is also attacked by grease.
w.2: EPDM swells and degrades with oils and fats.

mock1.q: When water-testing a low-slope roof to find a leak, where should testing begin?
o: Inside, by removing ceiling tiles only
At the lowest suspect component, then work upward one area at a time
At the highest point, flooding the whole roof at once
Anywhere, as long as a hose is used
mock1.e: Starting low and working up, one component at a time, means that when a leak appears, the water came from the area just tested, not from upslope water running down.

w.0: Interior observation helps, but it doesn't isolate the leak source on the roof.
w.2: Flooding from the top wets everything downslope and makes it impossible to isolate the leak.
w.3: Random testing gives ambiguous results.

mock1.src: NRCA Repair Manual practice (paywalled); industry leak-investigation practice

mock1.q: A company holding an Illinois LIMITED roofing license is asked to reroof a 12-unit apartment building. Which statement is correct?
o: The job requires an UNLIMITED license, because the limited license covers only residential properties of 8 units or less
The job is allowed if the building is under 3 stories
The limited license covers all residential buildings, regardless of size
The job is allowed if the company hires a subcontractor to install the flashing
mock1.e: A limited roofing license is for contractors whose business is limited to residential properties of 8 units or less. A 12-unit building exceeds that.

w.1: The Act uses unit count, not stories.
w.2: The limited license has an 8-unit cap.
w.3: Subcontracting part of the work doesn't expand the license scope.

mock1.q: What surety bond amount must an applicant for an UNLIMITED Illinois roofing license maintain?
mock1.e: The Act requires a continuous surety bond of $10,000 for a limited license and $25,000 for an unlimited license.

w.0: $5,000 is not a value in the Act.
w.1: $10,000 is the limited-license bond.
w.3: $50,000 is not the statutory amount.

mock1.q: What minimum public liability and property damage insurance do the Illinois roofing rules require?
o: $1,000,000 general aggregate only
$100,000 per person and $300,000 per occurrence
$250,000 per occurrence for property damage and $500,000 per occurrence for personal injury
$50,000 property damage and $100,000 bodily injury
mock1.e: 68 Ill. Adm. Code 1460.20 requires $250,000 per occurrence for property damage and $500,000 per occurrence for personal injury or bodily harm. The policy can't be cancelled without 30 days' written notice to the Division.

w.0: The rule specifies per-occurrence amounts.
w.1: $100,000/$300,000 matches part of the Home Repair and Remodeling Act's insurance provision, not the roofing rule.
w.3: These amounts are lower than the roofing rule requires.

mock1.q: A roofing contractor's surety wants to terminate the license bond. What happens under the Act?
o: The license continues until the next renewal, regardless of the bond
The surety files a 60-day notice with the Department and the contractor; the license is cancelled without hearing on the termination date unless a new bond takes effect
The contractor gets a 1-year grace period to replace the bond
The surety may cancel immediately without notice
mock1.e: A surety may terminate the bond by filing a 60-day notice of termination with the Department and sending notice to the contractor. The license is cancelled without hearing on the termination date unless a new bond is filed to take effect then.

w.0: The license can't continue without a bond in force.
w.2: The Act provides no grace period.
w.3: A 60-day notice is required.

mock1.q: Under the current Act, which arrangement is NOT permitted for a company's qualifying party?
o: Having the qualifying party be an officer of the corporation
Paying the qualifying party as a W-2 employee with withholding and workers' compensation
Having the qualifying party supervise installation operations
Paying the qualifying party as an independent contractor on a Form 1099
mock1.e: The qualifying party must be an employee who receives compensation from, and is under the supervision and control of, the licensee. The employer deducts FICA and withholding and provides workers' compensation. The qualifying party may not receive a Form 1099 from the licensee.

w.0: A qualifying party may be an officer, partner, or manager.
w.1: This is exactly what the Act requires.
w.2: The qualifying party must have authority to supervise roofing installation operations.

mock1.q: A company's qualifying party quits. Within what time must both the company and the former qualifying party notify the Department in writing?
o: 10 days
30 business days
60 days
7 months
mock1.e: Both the licensee and the qualifying party must notify the Department of the disassociation in writing, by mail or email, within 30 business days. Otherwise the license is placed on inoperative status.

w.0: 10 days is not the statutory period.
w.2: 60 days is the time to name a new qualifying party after notifying the Department.
w.3: 7 months is the time for the new qualifying party to pass the exam.

mock1.q: A newly designated qualifying party who hasn't passed the exam is approved by the Department. How long does that person have to pass it before the license becomes inoperative?
o: 30 days
60 days
7 months
2 years
mock1.e: Within 7 months after Department approval, the newly designated qualifying party must take and pass the examination. Otherwise the license is automatically placed on inoperative status until the company requalifies.

w.0: 30 days is not the exam period.
w.1: 60 days is the deadline to name a new qualifying party.
w.3: 2 years is not in the Act.

mock1.q: An individual is the qualifying party for ABC Roofing (unlimited license). Under what condition may that person also serve as qualifying party for a second licensee?
o: The second licensee holds the same type of license and shares common ownership or management of at least 25% (or is a licensed subsidiary)
The second company holds a limited license
The second company is in a different county
Never, under any circumstances
mock1.e: A person may act as qualifying party for one additional licensee of the same type of licensure. There must be common ownership or management of at least 25%, or the second company must be a licensed subsidiary (at least 25% owned or managed).

w.1: The additional licensee must hold the same TYPE of license.
w.2: Geography is irrelevant.
w.3: The Act allows one additional licensee under the stated conditions.

mock1.q: Under the Illinois Roofing Act, what rescission right must a roofing contract give the property owner?
o: No rescission right is required if the owner pays a deposit
The right to rescind within 30 days
The right to rescind only if an insurance claim is denied
The right to rescind and receive a full refund of any deposit within 72 hours after entering the contract
mock1.e: The contract must state the cancellation and refund policy. That includes a rescission clause allowing the owner to rescind within 72 hours after entering the contract and get a full refund of any deposit, plus a written statement that the owner may rescind.

w.0: The rescission clause is required.
w.1: 30 days is not the roofing-contract rescission period.
w.2: The insurance-denial cancellation right comes from the Home Repair and Remodeling Act. The Roofing Act separately requires the 72-hour clause.

mock1.q: The homeowner will pay for the roof with insurance proceeds. What must the roofing contract state about the deductible?
o: The contractor cannot pay, waive, rebate, or promise to pay, waive, or rebate any part of the insurance deductible
The contractor may rebate half the deductible
The contractor may waive the deductible if the owner signs a waiver
The contract need not mention the deductible
mock1.e: The Act requires a written statement that, when insurance proceeds will pay for the work, the contractor cannot pay, waive, rebate, or promise to pay, waive, or rebate any part of the deductible. The Home Repair and Remodeling Act also bars advertising or promising such rebates.

w.1: A partial rebate is still prohibited.
w.2: The owner's consent doesn't make the practice lawful.
w.3: The statement is a required contract term.

mock1.q: What must a roofing contract state, on its face and in bold type?
o: That the contractor is not responsible for leaks
The contractor's workers' compensation policy number
That the owner waives all lien rights
That the contractor will hold in trust any payment from the owner until materials are delivered to the site or a majority of the work is performed
mock1.e: Section 5.5(c) requires a bold-faced statement on the face of the contract. It says the contractor will hold in trust any owner payment until roofing materials are delivered or a majority of the work is performed.

w.0: A disclaimer of leak responsibility is not required and may be unenforceable.
w.1: The contract identifies the surety and liability insurer, but the bold statement is the trust statement.
w.2: Lien waivers are not a required contract statement.

mock1.q: What is the civil penalty for failing to display the roofing license number and licensee name on commercial vehicles?
mock1.e: Section 5.1 requires the license number and name on all commercial vehicles used in offering roofing services. Violations carry a civil penalty of not less than $250 and not more than $1,000. The Department, the Attorney General, or local code enforcement may enforce it.

w.0: $100 is not the statutory penalty.
w.2: $5,000 is not the vehicle penalty.
w.3: $15,000 is the maximum fine for disciplinary violations under §9.1, not the vehicle penalty.

mock1.q: A licensee knowingly runs a radio ad that omits the license number, and it airs for 5 days. What is the consequence under Section 5?
o: A Class A misdemeanor with a $1,000 fine, with each day the ad runs counted as a separate offense
A single $250 civil penalty
A warning letter only
No penalty, because radio ads are exempt
mock1.e: Knowingly failing to display the license number and name in advertising is a Class A misdemeanor with a $1,000 fine. Each day an advertisement runs is a separate offense, and administrative discipline can also apply.

w.1: $250 is the minimum for the vehicle-display violation.
w.2: The statute provides criminal penalties, not just warnings.
w.3: Advertising rules apply to all advertisements.

mock1.q: Under the Act as amended effective August 15, 2025, what is the maximum fine the Department may impose for each violation in a disciplinary action?
mock1.e: P.A. 104-427 raised the maximum disciplinary fine to $15,000 per violation. It was previously $10,000.

w.0: $1,000 is the advertising misdemeanor fine and the top of the vehicle penalty range.
w.1: $5,000 is not the statutory figure.
w.2: $10,000 was the maximum before the 2025 amendment.

mock1.q: Which of the following can be prima facie evidence of professional incompetence or gross negligence under the Act?
o: A court judgment against the contractor relating to roof work that results in leakage within 90 days after completion
A roof that leaks 10 years after installation
A bid that was higher than competitors'
A customer's online complaint about scheduling
mock1.e: Section 9.1 lists professional incompetence or gross negligence as grounds for discipline. Prima facie evidence may be a conviction or judgment relating to roof construction or repair that results in leakage within 90 days after the work is completed.

w.1: A leak 10 years later is not the 90-day standard.
w.2: Pricing is not a ground for discipline.
w.3: A scheduling complaint is not the statutory evidence standard.

mock1.q: A job's total cost (direct costs plus allocated overhead) is $32,000. The contractor wants a 20% profit MARGIN on the selling price. What should the price be?

w.0: $38,400 is a 20% MARKUP on cost, which is only a 16.7% margin.
w.1: $38,720 doesn't come from the margin formula.

mock1.q: A roofing company has current assets of $450,000 and current liabilities of $300,000. What is its current ratio?
mock1.e: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = 450,000 ÷ 300,000 = 1.50.

w.0: 0.67 inverts the ratio.
w.1: 1.33 is a calculation error.
