w.3: 2.50 is a calculation error.

mock1.q: A contractor has 12 employees, each earning more than $7,000 this year. The contractor qualifies for the full 5.4% state credit. What is the annual net FUTA tax?
mock1.e: FUTA is 6.0% of the first $7,000 per employee, less up to a 5.4% credit, for a net 0.6%. 0.006 × $7,000 = $42 per employee; × 12 = $504.

w.0: $84 covers only 2 employees.
w.2: $5,040 applies the full 6.0% rate without the credit.
w.3: $7,560 doesn't follow the FUTA formula.

mock1.q: A new roofer starts work on Monday. By when must the employer complete Section 2 of Form I-9, examining the employee's documents?
o: Within 30 days
By the end of the first pay period, whenever it falls
Within 3 business days of the first day of work
Before the job offer is made
mock1.e: The employee completes Section 1 by the first day of work. The employer completes Section 2 within 3 business days of the employee's first day of work.

w.0: 30 days is too long.
w.1: Pay periods vary, and the deadline is 3 business days.
w.3: I-9 documents are reviewed after hire, not before the offer.

mock1.q: On a public school roofing project, the contractor furnishes a payment bond. Whom does it primarily protect?
o: Subcontractors and material suppliers who aren't paid by the contractor
The contractor, if the owner doesn't pay
The surety, if the contractor goes bankrupt
The owner, if the roof leaks during the warranty period
mock1.e: A payment bond guarantees that subcontractors and suppliers get paid. That matters on public projects, where liens usually can't be placed on public property. A performance bond protects the owner against contractor default.

w.1: Bonds protect the obligee and claimants, not the principal (contractor).
w.2: The contractor must indemnify the surety; the bond doesn't protect the surety.
w.3: Owner protection is the purpose of the performance bond, and warranty issues are separate.

mock1.src: Surety practice (NASCLA-type content); Illinois Public Construction Bond Act (30 ILCS 550)

mock1.q: A specification calls for an "FM Class 1-90" roof assembly. What does the "90" indicate?
o: The maximum roof slope in degrees
The minimum R-value
The assembly's wind-uplift resistance rating (in pounds per square foot) in FM testing
The fire rating in minutes
mock1.e: FM Approvals uplift classes (1-60, 1-75, 1-90, and so on) indicate the uplift pressure, in psf, the assembly withstood in testing. "Class 1" refers to the fire and wind classification.

w.0: It isn't a slope.
w.1: It isn't an insulation value.
w.3: The number is not a fire-endurance time.

mock1.src: FM Approvals / FM Global Data Sheets 1-28, 1-29

mock1.q: Which area of a low-slope roof typically experiences the HIGHEST wind uplift pressure and needs the most enhanced attachment?
o: The corners
Around drains
The field (center)
The perimeter midpoints only
mock1.e: Wind uplift is highest at corners, next highest along perimeters, and lowest in the field. Attachment is increased in corner and perimeter zones.

w.1: Drains are not a wind zone.
w.2: The field has the lowest design pressure.
w.3: Perimeters are high, but corners are higher.

mock1.q: A mechanically attached single-ply roof over a steel deck shows small "tents" in the membrane directly over some insulation fasteners, and one has punctured the membrane. What is the most likely cause?
o: Fastener back-out from deck movement or fasteners that didn't properly engage the steel deck
Too much adhesive
UV degradation
Ponding water
mock1.e: When screws don't engage the deck properly, or cyclic deck movement and vibration work them loose, they back out and push up through the insulation and into the membrane.

w.1: Adhesive quantity doesn't push fasteners up.
w.2: UV damages the surface. It does not push fasteners up.
w.3: Ponding causes other damage, not tenting at fasteners.

mock1.src: NRCA practice; fastener manufacturer requirements (penetration through steel deck)

mock1.q: Which method is commonly used to adhere polyiso insulation boards to a structural concrete deck without hot asphalt?
o: Roofing staples
Water-based latex paint
Loose-laid boards, with no attachment and no ballast
Low-rise polyurethane foam adhesive, in beads or full coverage per the manufacturer's pattern
mock1.e: Low-rise foam adhesives are widely used to adhere insulation to concrete and other substrates. Bead spacing is set by the manufacturer and the wind zone.

w.0: Staples can't attach insulation to concrete.
w.1: Paint is not an adhesive.
w.2: Loose-laid insulation needs ballast.

mock1.q: A new roof covers an indoor swimming pool with a steel deck. Which assembly feature is MOST critical?
o: A reflective white membrane
Extra insulation fasteners in the field only
Ballast instead of adhesive
A continuous vapor retarder on the warm (interior) side of the insulation, installed over a substrate board and sealed at all edges and penetrations
mock1.e: Pools create very high interior humidity. A continuous, sealed vapor retarder on the warm side keeps moisture out of the insulation. Over steel, it goes on a substrate board. Air leaks at the edges and penetrations must be sealed.

w.0: Reflectivity doesn't address the moisture drive.
w.1: Fasteners don't control vapor, and they add penetrations through the vapor retarder.
w.2: Ballast doesn't control vapor.

mock1.src: NRCA condensation guidance (paywalled); building science practice

mock1.q: In a freezer warehouse kept at −10°F, which direction is the dominant vapor drive through the roof?
o: There is no vapor drive in cold storage
From the interior toward the outside
Only upward, regardless of temperature
From outside toward the cold interior
mock1.e: Vapor moves from warm, moist air toward cold, dry air. In cold storage the exterior is warmer and wetter, so the vapor retarder function belongs on the exterior (warm) side, often the membrane itself.

w.0: A large temperature difference creates a strong vapor drive.
w.1: That's the normal direction for a heated building, which is reversed here.
w.2: Vapor drive follows temperature and vapor pressure, not a fixed direction.

mock1.src: Building science practice; NRCA condensation guidance (paywalled)

mock1.q: Why do structural standing-seam metal roof systems use sliding (expansion) clips?
o: They let the panels be installed without a fixed point
They allow the panels to expand and contract lengthwise with temperature changes, without tearing the fasteners
They increase the fire rating
They eliminate the need for end laps
mock1.e: Long metal panels move significantly with temperature. Sliding clips let the panel move while holding it down. A designated fixed point controls where movement starts.

w.0: Systems still have a fixed point; sliding clips work together with it.
w.2: Clips don't affect the fire rating.
w.3: End laps are still needed on long runs, per the manufacturer.

mock1.src: Metal panel manufacturer design guides; NRCA Metal Panel manual (paywalled)

mock1.q: In a pre-engineered metal building, faced fiberglass blanket insulation is draped over the purlins under the roof panels. Which way should the vapor-retarder facing face?
o: It should be removed so the insulation can breathe
Either way, because metal buildings don't condense
Toward the roof panels (cold side)
Toward the heated interior (warm side), with the facing seams sealed
mock1.e: The facing is the vapor retarder, so it goes on the warm-in-winter side, facing the interior. Its seams are sealed or taped so moist interior air can't reach the cold metal panel and condense.

w.0: Removing the facing removes the vapor control.
w.1: Metal buildings are prone to condensation.
w.2: Facing the cold side traps moisture in the insulation.

mock1.src: NAIMA / metal building insulation guidance; building science practice

mock1.q: A newly sprayed SPF roof surface looks like "popcorn," with deep voids between rounded nodules. What is the correct response?
o: Accept it, because texture doesn't matter under a coating
Cover it with gravel
Apply a double coat of coating over it
Reject the surface; remove the popcorn texture and respray before coating
mock1.e: Smooth, orange-peel, and coarse orange-peel textures are acceptable for coating. Popcorn and tree-bark textures aren't, because coatings can't fully cover the voids and water collects. The surface must be corrected.

w.0: Texture is a key SPF quality criterion.
w.1: Gravel doesn't fix a defective foam surface.
w.2: Extra coating can't reliably fill deep voids.

mock1.src: SPF industry guidance; manufacturer specifications; NRCA SPF manual (paywalled)

mock1.q: Under common SPF manufacturer guidance, which condition should stop spray foam application?
o: The substrate is clean, dry concrete
The substrate surface temperature is within about 5°F of the dew point
The air temperature is 70°F with light wind
The sky is overcast but dry
mock1.e: Moisture on the substrate ruins adhesion and causes blistering. Most manufacturers require the surface to be dry and at least about 5°F above the dew point.

w.0: Clean, dry concrete is a suitable substrate.
w.2: 70°F with light wind is generally acceptable.
w.3: Overcast, dry conditions don't by themselves prevent spraying.

mock1.q: A roof coating is 50% solids by volume, and the specification requires 15 dry mils. One gallon over 100 sq ft yields about 16 wet mils. About how many gallons are needed for 80 squares, before waste?
o: 75 gal
120 gal
150 gal
240 gal
mock1.e: Wet mils needed = 15 ÷ 0.50 = 30 wet mils. Gallons per square = 30 ÷ 16 ≈ 1.875. For 80 squares: 1.875 × 80 = 150 gal.

w.0: 75 gal treats dry mils as wet mils (15 ÷ 16 × 80).
w.1: 120 gal assumes 1.5 gal per square.
w.3: 240 gal assumes 3 gal per square.

mock1.src: Coating calculation (1 gal = 231 cu in; 231 ÷ 14,400 sq in ≈ 0.016 in = 16 mils)

mock1.q: In a protected membrane roof (PMR/IRMA), what insulation is placed ABOVE the membrane?
o: Polyisocyanurate with paper facers
Extruded polystyrene (XPS)
Wood fiberboard
Perlite board
mock1.e: In a PMR, the insulation is over the membrane and gets periodically wet. XPS is used because of its low water absorption. It is then covered with fabric and ballast or pavers.

w.2: Fiberboard absorbs water and would fail.
w.3: Perlite absorbs water and would fail.

mock1.q: What distinguishes waterproofing from dampproofing on a below-grade wall?
o: Waterproofing resists water under hydrostatic pressure; dampproofing only resists moisture without hydrostatic pressure
They are the same thing
Dampproofing is applied on the interior, and waterproofing on the exterior
Waterproofing is only used on roofs
mock1.e: Waterproofing is designed to resist water under hydrostatic head. Dampproofing only retards moisture and vapor where there is no hydrostatic pressure.

w.1: They are different in performance and use.
w.2: Both are usually applied on the positive (exterior) side. Location isn't the distinction.
w.3: Waterproofing is used below grade and on plaza decks, as well as on roofs.

mock1.src: NRCA Waterproofing Manual (2005, paywalled; not read); industry definitions

mock1.q: A hot-asphalt BUR reroof is scheduled on an occupied hospital. What is the MOST important coordination step to protect the occupants?
o: Increase the kettle temperature so the asphalt cures faster
Coordinate with the owner to shut down or seal rooftop air intakes near the work, and schedule work to limit fumes entering the building
Open all roof hatches for ventilation
Work only at night, without telling the owner
mock1.e: Asphalt fumes and odors drawn into air intakes can affect occupants, especially in sensitive facilities. Coordinated intake shutdown or sealing, scheduling, and low-fume equipment are standard practice.

w.2: Open hatches let fumes into the building.
w.3: Working without owner coordination risks exposing occupants.

mock1.q: New rooftop mechanical equipment will sit on raised supports over a membrane roof. How should the clearance under the equipment be set, per NRCA-style guidance?
o: High enough for roofers to reach under and replace the roof. Wider equipment needs more clearance
No clearance; set the equipment directly on the membrane
The same fixed 6-in clearance for all equipment sizes
As low as possible, to reduce wind loads
mock1.e: NRCA publishes minimum clearances that increase with equipment width, because a roofer must reach farther under wider units to install and repair flashings and membrane.

w.2: One fixed small clearance doesn't allow for wide units.
w.3: Clearance is driven by maintenance and reroofing access, not by minimizing height.

mock1.src: NRCA Membrane manual (equipment support guidance; paywalled; principle widely published)

mock2.q: A crew is replacing the membrane on a low-slope warehouse roof that is 160 ft wide. Which fall-protection arrangement is permitted for the roofing work?
o: A safety monitoring system alone
A warning line system combined with a safety monitoring system for workers between the line and the edge
A warning line system alone
Verbal reminders from the foreman at the start of each shift
mock2.e: On a low-slope roof wider than 50 ft, a safety monitor alone isn't permitted. The permitted options include guardrails, nets, or PFAS, or a warning line combined with one of those systems or with a safety monitor.

w.0: A monitor alone is limited to roofs 50 ft or less in width.
w.2: A warning line is never a stand-alone system.
w.3: Verbal reminders aren't a fall-protection system.

mock2.q: Which arrangement VIOLATES OSHA's requirements for a safety monitor?
o: The monitor has no other job duties while monitoring
The monitor is a competent person on the same roof surface as the crew
The monitor is close enough to warn workers by voice
The monitor watches the crew from the parking lot and warns them by two-way radio
mock2.e: A safety monitor must be on the same walking/working surface, within visual sighting distance of the employees, and close enough to communicate orally. A monitor in the parking lot with a radio doesn't meet this.

w.0: This is a requirement: no other responsibilities that could distract from monitoring.
w.1: This is a requirement.
w.2: This is a requirement.

mock2.q: Which top-rail height is NOT compliant for a guardrail system on a roof edge (no stilts in use)?
o: 37 in
40 in
42 in
45 in
mock2.e: Top rails must be 42 in plus or minus 3 in above the walking/working level, which is 39 to 45 in. 37 in is too low.

w.1: 40 in is within the 39–45 in range.
w.2: 42 in is the nominal height.
w.3: 45 in is the upper limit and is compliant.

mock2.q: A top rail must withstand what force applied within 2 in of its top edge, outward or downward?
o: 50 lb
150 lb
200 lb
mock2.e: Guardrail systems must withstand at least 200 lb applied within 2 in of the top edge in any outward or downward direction. Midrails must withstand 150 lb, and toeboards 50 lb.

w.0: 50 lb is the toeboard requirement.
w.1: 150 lb is the midrail requirement.
w.3: 5,000 lb is the PFAS anchorage requirement.

mock2.q: Where toeboards are used to keep tools and materials from falling off a roof edge, what is their minimum height?
o: 2 in
3½ in
6 in
12 in
mock2.e: Toeboards must be at least 3½ in high (top edge to walking/working surface) and withstand at least 50 lb.

w.0: 2 in is too low.
w.2: 6 in exceeds the minimum.
w.3: 12 in exceeds the minimum.

mock2.q: A 30 × 30 in opening in a roof deck is covered with plywood. Which set of conditions makes the cover compliant?
o: It supports at least twice the imposed load, is secured against displacement, and is marked "HOLE" or "COVER"
It is covered by a tarp so debris doesn't fall in
It is ⅜-in plywood laid loose over the hole
It is painted orange, and workers are told about it
mock2.e: Covers must support at least twice the weight of employees, equipment, and materials imposed. They must be secured so they can't be displaced, and marked with the word "HOLE" or "COVER" (or color-coded).

w.1: A tarp is not a cover and hides the hazard.
w.2: A loose, thin cover can shift or break.
w.3: Paint and verbal warnings don't meet the strength and securing requirements.

mock2.q: What is the greatest distance a safety net may be installed below the working surface?
o: 6 ft
15 ft
25 ft
30 ft
mock2.e: Safety nets must be installed as close as practicable under the work, but never more than 30 ft below it.

w.0: 6 ft is the general fall-protection trigger height.
w.1: 15 ft is not the net rule.
w.2: 25 ft is the maximum control-line distance from a leading edge, not the net distance.

mock2.q: A worker wants to use a body belt instead of a full-body harness with his lanyard for fall arrest. What is the correct answer?
o: Body belts are allowed if the lanyard is shock-absorbing
Body belts aren't acceptable as part of a personal fall arrest system; a full-body harness is required
Body belts are allowed on low-slope roofs only
Body belts are allowed if the free fall is under 6 ft
mock2.e: Since January 1, 1998, body belts may not be used as part of a personal fall arrest system. They are allowed only in positioning systems.

w.0: A shock-absorbing lanyard doesn't make a body belt acceptable for arrest.
w.2: There is no low-slope exception.
w.3: Free-fall distance doesn't create an exception.

mock2.q: What type of snaphook may be used in a personal fall arrest system?
o: Locking-type snaphooks only
Snaphooks aren't allowed; only carabiners
Non-locking snaphooks, if they are inspected daily
Any snaphook with a spring gate
mock2.e: Only locking-type snaphooks, designed and used to prevent disengagement, are permitted. Non-locking snaphooks have been prohibited since 1998.

w.1: Locking snaphooks are standard PFAS connectors.
w.2: Daily inspection doesn't make a non-locking hook acceptable.
w.3: A plain spring gate can roll out and disengage.

mock2.q: What minimum breaking strength must a self-retracting lifeline that automatically limits free fall to 2 ft or less have?
mock2.e: Self-retracting lifelines and lanyards that automatically limit free fall to 2 ft or less must have a tensile strength of at least 3,000 lb. Those that don't must meet 5,000 lb.

w.0: 1,800 lb is the maximum arresting force.
w.2: 3,600 lb is the snaphook/D-ring proof test.
w.3: 5,000 lb applies to ordinary lanyards and to SRLs that don't limit free fall to 2 ft.

mock2.q: A roofer uses a 6-ft shock-absorbing lanyard attached to an anchor at the height of his back D-ring. Allow 3.5 ft of deceleration, 1 ft of harness stretch, 5 ft from the D-ring to the feet, and a 2-ft safety margin. The ground is 14 ft below the anchor. Is the clearance adequate?
o: Yes; only 12 ft is needed
No; about 17.5 ft of clearance is needed
No; about 25 ft is needed
Yes; only 9.5 ft is needed
mock2.e: Required clearance = 6 (free fall) + 3.5 (deceleration) + 1 (stretch) + 5 (D-ring to feet) + 2 (margin) = 17.5 ft. With only 14 ft, the worker could strike the ground. A self-retracting lifeline or different anchoring is needed.

w.0: 12 ft leaves out the body length below the D-ring and the margin.
w.2: 25 ft overstates the requirement.
w.3: 9.5 ft counts only free fall and deceleration.

mock2.src: 29 CFR 1926.502(d)(16) (no contact with lower level; 6-ft free fall; 3.5-ft deceleration); ANSI Z359 clearance method

mock2.q: What must the employer's written certification record of fall-protection training contain?
o: The name of the employee trained, the date(s) of training, and the signature of the trainer or employer
The employee's social security number and home address
A copy of the employee's driver's license
Only the name of the training company
mock2.e: The certification record must include the name or other identity of the employee trained, the date(s) of training, and the signature of the person who conducted the training or of the employer.

w.1: SSN and address aren't required elements.
w.2: A license copy isn't required.
w.3: The record must identify the employee and the date and be signed.

mock2.q: In which situation may an employer use a written fall protection plan instead of guardrails, nets, or PFAS?
o: Any roof lower than 20 ft
Whenever workers are experienced roofers
Any commercial reroof, if the owner agrees
Residential construction, when the employer can show conventional fall protection is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, with the plan prepared by a qualified person
mock2.e: Fall protection plans are allowed only for leading-edge work, precast concrete erection, and residential construction, and only where conventional protection is infeasible or creates a greater hazard. The plan must be site-specific and prepared by a qualified person.

w.0: Height alone doesn't qualify a job.
w.1: Experience doesn't qualify a job.
w.2: Commercial reroofing doesn't qualify, and owner agreement doesn't matter.

mock2.q: An extension ladder gives access to a roof. How far must the side rails extend above the roof edge (upper landing surface)?
o: 1 ft
2 ft
3 ft
5 ft
mock2.e: Portable ladders used to reach an upper landing must have side rails that extend at least 3 ft above it. Where that isn't possible, the ladder is secured at the top and a grasping device is provided.

w.0: 1 ft is too short.
w.1: 2 ft is too short.
w.3: 5 ft is more than the minimum.

mock2.q: Which use of a stepladder is prohibited?
o: Standing on the top step
Using a fiberglass stepladder near electrical equipment
Using it on a level, stable surface
Using it fully opened with the spreaders locked
mock2.e: The top or top step of a stepladder may not be used as a step. Stepladders must also be fully opened and locked, and used on stable, level surfaces.

w.1: Nonconductive rails are the correct choice near electrical equipment.
w.2: Stable, level footing is required.
w.3: Fully opened with locked spreaders is the required setup.

mock2.t: When stairways or ladders are required
mock2.q: A stairway or ladder must be provided at a break in elevation of at least how much, when no ramp, runway, embankment, or hoist is available?
o: 12 in
19 in
24 in
36 in
mock2.e: A stairway or ladder is required at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 in or more, and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided.

w.0: 12 in is below the threshold.
w.2: 24 in is above the threshold.
w.3: 36 in is above the threshold.

mock2.q: Workers are on a supported scaffold erected to tear off a mansard. At what platform height does OSHA's scaffold standard require fall protection?
o: 4 ft
6 ft
10 ft
15 ft
mock2.e: Under the scaffold standard, employees on a scaffold more than 10 ft above a lower level need fall protection.

w.0: 4 ft is the general-industry threshold, not the construction scaffold rule.
w.1: 6 ft is the Subpart M threshold for roofs and edges, not scaffolds.
w.3: 15 ft is not the scaffold rule.

mock2.q: How often must a competent person inspect a scaffold for visible defects?
o: Once when it is erected
Before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect its structural integrity
Only after a storm
Weekly
mock2.e: Scaffolds and their components must be inspected by a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity.

w.0: A single inspection at erection is not enough.
w.2: Storms are one trigger, but inspection is also required every shift.
w.3: Weekly is not frequent enough.

mock2.q: According to OSHA and NIOSH nail gun guidance, which trigger type provides the greatest protection against unintended firing and double-fire injuries?
o: Full sequential trigger
Contact (bump) trigger
Single-shot contact trigger
Any trigger, if the operator wears safety glasses
mock2.e: A full sequential trigger fires only when the safety contact is pressed first and then the trigger is squeezed. It greatly reduces unintended discharges. Contact triggers have about twice the injury risk.

w.1: Contact (bump) triggers are the highest-risk type.
w.2: Single-shot contact triggers are still less protective than full sequential.
w.3: Glasses protect the eyes but don't prevent unintended firing.

mock2.src: OSHA/NIOSH "Nail Gun Safety: A Guide for Construction Contractors" (2011)

mock2.q: A worker wants to blow debris off the roof with compressed air. Under what condition does OSHA permit compressed air for cleaning?
o: Only when the pressure is reduced to less than 30 psi, with effective chip guarding and PPE
At any pressure, if the worker wears gloves
Never under any circumstances
Only above 90 psi, to be effective
mock2.e: Compressed air may be used for cleaning only where it is reduced to less than 30 psi, and then only with effective chip guarding and personal protective equipment.

w.1: Gloves don't make high-pressure cleaning acceptable.
w.2: It is permitted under the stated conditions.
w.3: Higher pressure increases the hazard and isn't permitted.

mock2.q: A worker will carry hot asphalt in buckets and mop it. Which PPE ensemble is MOST appropriate?
o: Short sleeves for cooling, cotton gloves, and sneakers
Long sleeves, gauntlet-style gloves, boots with pant legs outside, safety glasses, and a face shield
A hard hat only
A respirator only
mock2.e: Hot asphalt causes severe burns. Cover the skin completely with long sleeves and gauntlet gloves, and wear boots with the pant legs outside so hot material can't run into them. Protect the eyes and face with safety glasses and a face shield.

w.0: Exposed skin and sneakers invite burns.
w.2: A hard hat doesn't protect skin or eyes from splashes.
w.3: Respiratory protection doesn't address burn hazards.

mock2.src: NRCA safety practice (paywalled; not read); 29 CFR 1926.95, 1926.102

mock2.q: A roofer will cut concrete roof tiles with a handheld power saw outdoors. Which control does OSHA's silica standard (Table 1) rely on for this task?
o: Cutting only in the morning, when silica levels are lower
A saw equipped with integrated water delivery that continuously feeds water to the blade
Dry cutting upwind of other workers
A paper dust mask with no other controls
mock2.e: For handheld power saws cutting silica-containing materials, Table 1 specifies integrated water delivery to the blade. Respirator requirements depend on the task's duration.

w.0: Time of day doesn't control silica exposure.
w.2: Standing upwind isn't a Table 1 engineering control.
w.3: A dust mask without engineering controls isn't the Table 1 method and isn't an approved respirator.

mock2.q: What is OSHA's permissible exposure limit (8-hour TWA) for asbestos in construction?
o: 0.1 f/cc
1.0 f/cc
5.0 f/cc
mock2.e: The asbestos PEL is 0.1 fiber per cubic centimeter as an 8-hour time-weighted average. The excursion limit is 1.0 f/cc averaged over 30 minutes.

w.0: 0.01 f/cc is not the PEL.
w.2: 1.0 f/cc is the 30-minute excursion limit.
w.3: 5.0 f/cc is far above any current limit.

mock2.q: More than 5 gallons of solvent-based adhesive are in use on a roof. Where must a fire extinguisher rated at least 10B be located?
o: Within 50 ft of where the flammable liquid is being used
Within 100 ft, anywhere on the site
On the ground floor of the building
In the foreman's truck
mock2.e: At least one extinguisher rated not less than 10B must be within 50 ft of wherever more than 5 gallons of flammable or combustible liquids, or 5 lb of flammable gas, are being used on the jobsite.

w.1: 100 ft is the travel-distance limit for the 2A building extinguishers, not this rule.
w.2: The ground floor may be far more than 50 ft from the roof work.
w.3: A truck may not be within 50 ft or accessible.

mock2.q: At the end of the day, where may full propane cylinders for torch-applied roofing be stored?
o: Inside any locked room of the building
Inside the building's stairwell, to keep them secure
In the building's mechanical room
Outside, in a storage area meeting OSHA separation requirements — not inside the building
mock2.e: OSHA prohibits storing LP-gas containers inside buildings. They must be stored outside, following the separation requirements for the quantity stored.

w.0: Locking a room doesn't change the prohibition.
w.1: A stairwell is inside a building and is a critical exit path.
w.2: A mechanical room is inside the building.

mock2.q: What gap does APA recommend between the edges and ends of plywood or OSB roof sheathing panels?
o: No gap
⅛ in
½ in
1 in
mock2.e: A ⅛-in gap at panel ends and edges lets the panels expand with moisture without buckling. Tight panels can ridge, and the ridging telegraphs through the shingles.

w.0: Tight joints cause buckling as the panels swell.
w.2: ½ in is excessive and leaves unsupported shingle areas.
w.3: 1 in is excessive.

mock2.src: APA Engineered Wood Construction Guide; manufacturer panel stamps

mock2.q: Why are H-clips (panel edge clips) used between rafters on some roof sheathing?
o: To hold the underlayment down in wind
To support the unsupported panel edges between framing members and keep the gap
To ground the roof for lightning protection
To attach the shingles to the deck
mock2.e: Panel clips support the edges of adjacent panels between rafters or trusses, where the span rating calls for edge support. They reduce deflection at the joints and set the spacing.

w.0: Underlayment is fastened separately.
w.2: H-clips aren't lightning protection.
w.3: Shingles are nailed to the deck, not clipped.

mock2.q: Rain soaked the exposed plywood deck overnight during a tear-off. What is the BEST course of action before installing underlayment and shingles?
o: Install underlayment immediately to protect the wet deck
Install the shingles directly on the wet deck without underlayment
Spray the deck with roof coating to seal the moisture in
Let the deck dry (replacing any delaminated or damaged panels) before covering it
mock2.e: Covering a wet deck traps moisture. The underlayment wrinkles, the panels swell and buckle, and the shingles can blister or buckle. Dry the deck and replace damaged panels first.

w.0: Covering a wet deck traps the water.
w.1: Underlayment is required, and the deck is still wet.
w.2: Coating traps moisture and isn't a steep-slope practice.

mock2.src: NRCA steep-slope practice; manufacturer requirements (dry deck)

mock2.q: What does a nuclear moisture gauge actually detect in a roof survey?
o: The weight of the insulation
Electrical capacitance of the membrane
Hydrogen atoms, most of which come from water in the assembly
Surface temperature differences
mock2.e: A nuclear gauge emits fast neutrons that slow when they strike hydrogen atoms. The counts rise with hydrogen, mostly from water, though some insulations and asphalt add a baseline.

w.0: Weight isn't measured.
w.1: Capacitance is used by capacitance/impedance meters.
w.3: Surface temperature is what infrared thermography measures.

mock2.q: When is an infrared roof moisture survey usually most effective?
o: At noon on a sunny day
During a light rain
In the evening after a sunny day, on a dry roof with low wind
Early morning after a cloudy day
mock2.e: Wet insulation stores more solar heat during the day and releases it slowly. After sunset, wet areas show up warmer than dry areas. Surface water and wind interfere with the reading.

w.0: At noon the sun heats the whole surface and masks the differences.
w.1: Surface water ruins the readings.
w.3: Without solar loading, there is little heat difference to see.

mock2.src: ASTM C1153; NRCA moisture survey practice

mock2.q: An owner wants asphalt shingles installed directly over an existing clay tile roof. What is the correct response under the model codes?
o: Not permitted; the tile must be removed first
Permitted if the tile is not cracked
Permitted with longer nails
Permitted with double underlayment
mock2.e: The model codes prohibit installing new coverings over existing slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile. Tile isn't a suitable nail base, and the combined weight is a concern.

w.1: Tile condition doesn't lift the prohibition.
w.2: Nail length doesn't make the re-cover allowable.
w.3: Underlayment doesn't make the re-cover allowable.

mock2.q: A dark-colored standing-seam roof will go over a self-adhered underlayment on a south-facing slope. What type of underlayment should be specified?
o: A high-temperature-rated self-adhered underlayment
No underlayment; metal is waterproof
The standard ice-barrier grade used under shingles
No. 15 felt only
mock2.e: Temperatures under metal roofing get very high. Standard-grade self-adhered membranes can soften, flow, and stick to the panels, which restricts their thermal movement. High-temperature grades are made for this.

w.1: Architectural metal panels need underlayment.
w.2: A standard grade may bleed or flow at metal-roof temperatures.
w.3: Organic felt can stick to hot metal and doesn't provide self-adhered protection where it's needed.

mock2.src: Underlayment and metal panel manufacturer instructions [MANUFACTURER]

mock2.q: A synthetic underlayment has been left exposed while the shingle delivery is delayed. What decides how long it may stay exposed to sunlight?
o: Code requires 12 months for all synthetics
The manufacturer's published UV exposure limit for that product
There is no limit; synthetics are UV-stable forever
24 hours for all products
mock2.e: UV exposure limits vary by product, often from about 30 to 180 days. The manufacturer's limit governs. Past it, the underlayment may need replacing.

w.0: No universal 12-month code rule exists.
w.2: Synthetics degrade with UV.
w.3: No universal 24-hour rule exists.

mock2.src: ICC-ES AC188 evaluation reports; manufacturer data [MANUFACTURER]

mock2.q: A roofer plans to patch a coal-tar pitch built-up roof with asphalt-based materials. What is the concern?
o: Coal tar can only be repaired with EPDM
None; all bitumens are interchangeable
Coal tar and asphalt are generally incompatible, so the repair materials must be compatible with coal tar
Asphalt will make the coal tar too hard
mock2.e: Coal tar and asphalt are chemically incompatible, and mixing them can cause softening, poor adhesion, and failure. Repairs must use coal-tar-compatible materials or a manufacturer-approved method.

w.0: EPDM is incompatible with bitumens unless it is separated.
w.1: Bitumens aren't interchangeable.
w.3: The concern is incompatibility and poor bonding, not simple hardening.

mock2.q: What does the equiviscous temperature (EVT) of roofing asphalt represent?
o: The temperature at which the asphalt reaches the viscosity for proper application
The maximum safe storage temperature
The temperature at which the asphalt ignites
The temperature at which the asphalt begins to soften on the roof
mock2.e: EVT is the temperature at which the asphalt has the right viscosity for mopping (or for mechanical spreading). Asphalt is applied at EVT ±25°F.

w.1: The storage limit relates to the flash point and the finished blowing temperature (FBT).
w.2: Ignition relates to the flash point.
w.3: Softening relates to the softening point.

mock2.src: NRCA BUR practice; asphalt bill of lading

mock2.q: Asphalt is held in a kettle well above its finished blowing temperature for many hours. What is the likely effect on the roof?
o: The asphalt becomes compatible with coal tar
The asphalt becomes stronger and more slip-resistant
No effect as long as the flash point isn't reached
The asphalt's softening point can drop, increasing the risk of slippage
mock2.e: Prolonged overheating changes asphalt's properties. It can lower the softening point, making the finished membrane more prone to flow and slippage, and it increases fumes and fire risk.

w.0: Overheating doesn't change compatibility with coal tar.
w.1: Overheating degrades asphalt; it doesn't strengthen it.
w.2: Quality is affected well below the flash point.

mock2.src: NRCA BUR practice; asphalt manufacturer guidance

mock2.q: Why is a cover board often installed over foam insulation beneath an adhered single-ply membrane?
o: It replaces the need for a vapor retarder
It reduces the membrane's weight
It adds most of the assembly's R-value
It provides a stable surface and improves resistance to foot traffic, hail, and fire
mock2.e: Cover boards (gypsum, high-density polyiso, perlite, fiberboard) protect the foam. They provide a smooth, strong substrate for adhesion and improve impact, traffic, and fire performance.

w.0: They don't serve as vapor retarders unless specifically designed to.
w.1: They add weight.
w.2: Cover boards add little R-value.

mock2.src: NRCA membrane practice; cover-board manufacturer data

mock2.q: At the end of the day, a temporary water cut-off (night seal) was installed where the new insulation and membrane stop. What must happen when work resumes?
o: Cut small drain holes in it
Leave it in place under the new membrane as a permanent seal
Cover it with extra insulation
Remove the night seal before continuing the new roof across that line
mock2.e: Night seals are temporary. If left in place, they can become dams that trap water and cause blisters or wet insulation under the new membrane.

w.0: Drain holes defeat the seal and don't solve the buried-dam problem.
w.1: Leaving it in creates a buried dam.
w.2: Burying it causes the same problem.

mock2.q: Why does NRCA recommend two or more layers of insulation with staggered (offset) joints rather than a single thick layer?
o: Single layers aren't allowed by code
Offset joints reduce thermal bridging and air movement through the board joints
Offsetting joints makes the roof steeper
Two layers are always cheaper
mock2.e: Joints through a single layer create continuous paths for heat loss and air (and moisture) movement. Offset joints in multiple layers block those paths.

w.0: Codes don't generally prohibit single layers.
w.2: Offsetting joints has nothing to do with slope.
w.3: Multiple layers usually cost more to install.

mock2.q: A roof must reach R-30 using polyiso rated at R-5.7 per inch, ignoring the cover board. What is the minimum total polyiso thickness, to the nearest tenth of an inch?
o: 4.5 in
5.3 in
5.7 in
6.0 in
mock2.e: Thickness = R ÷ (R per inch) = 30 ÷ 5.7 = 5.26 in, which rounds to about 5.3 in. In practice this is two layers, such as 2.6 in + 2.7 in, or the next available product thicknesses.

w.0: 4.5 in gives only R-25.7.
w.2: 5.7 in treats the R per inch as the thickness.
w.3: 6.0 in exceeds the minimum.

mock2.q: Tapered insulation slopes at ¼ in per foot toward a drain 48 ft from the high point. The minimum thickness at the drain is ½ in. What is the thickness at the high point, excluding any flat base layers?
o: 6.0 in
mock2.e: Rise = 48 ft × 0.25 in/ft = 12 in. Add the ½-in starter: 12 + 0.5 = 12.5 in.

w.0: 6.0 in uses ⅛ in per ft.
w.1: 12.0 in forgets the ½-in starter thickness.
w.3: 24.5 in uses ½ in per ft.

mock2.q: Galvanized steel flashing installed under red cedar shingles is corroding prematurely. What is the most likely cause?
o: UV exposure
Condensation from the attic only
Too many nails
Tannic acid leaching from the cedar attacks the zinc coating
mock2.e: Cedar leaches tannic acid when wet, and it corrodes zinc and galvanized coatings. Copper or stainless flashing is preferred with cedar.

w.0: The flashing is under the shingles, out of the UV.
w.1: Condensation isn't the typical cause in this pairing.
w.2: Nail count doesn't cause coating corrosion.

mock2.src: Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau guidance; NRCA metal practice

mock2.q: A house has a plan area (including overhangs) of 1,800 sq ft. The roof is a 5:12 slope (factor 1.083). What is the actual roof area in squares, before waste?

w.0: 18.0 squares ignores the slope.
w.2: 20.2 squares uses the 6:12 factor (1.118).
w.3: 22.5 squares uses a factor of 1.25 (9:12).

mock2.q: An 8:12 roof slope corresponds to what roof PITCH (rise ÷ span)?
mock2.e: Pitch = rise ÷ span. The span is twice the run, so pitch = 8 ÷ 24 = 1/3.

w.0: 1/4 pitch corresponds to a 6:12 slope.
w.2: 2/3 is the rise-to-run ratio (8:12), which is the slope, not the pitch.
w.3: 8/12 is the slope expressed as a fraction, not the pitch.

mock2.q: A 26-square roof slope of 4:12 or steeper needs single-layer No. 15 felt. The rolls nominally cover 4 squares. How many rolls should be ordered?
mock2.e: 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5, which rounds up to 7 rolls.

w.0: 6 rolls rounds down and leaves the roof short.
w.2: 13 rolls uses the 2-squares-per-roll coverage of No. 30 felt.
w.3: 26 rolls treats each roll as covering one square.

mock2.q: Which ASTM D7158 classification indicates the HIGHEST wind resistance for asphalt shingles?
o: Class D
Class F
Class G
Class H
mock2.e: ASTM D7158 classes are D (about 90 mph), G (about 120 mph), and H (about 150 mph). Class H is the highest.

w.0: Class D is the lowest D7158 class.
w.1: Class F belongs to ASTM D3161, a different test standard.
w.2: Class G is in the middle.

mock2.q: An owner in a hail-prone area asks for the most impact-resistant asphalt shingle rating. What should the contractor specify?
o: UL 2218 Class 1
UL 2218 Class 2
UL 2218 Class 3
UL 2218 Class 4
mock2.e: UL 2218 rates impact resistance from Class 1 to Class 4. Class 4 is the most resistant, and some insurers offer discounts for it.

w.0: Class 1 is the lowest.
w.1: Class 2 is lower than Class 4.
w.2: Class 3 is lower than Class 4.

mock2.q: Which roof covering fire classification (ASTM E108 / UL 790) indicates the BEST resistance to external fire?
o: Class A
Class B
Class C
Class D
mock2.e: Class A indicates effectiveness against severe fire exposure. Class B is moderate and Class C is light. Most asphalt shingles are Class A.

w.1: Class B is lower.
w.2: Class C is the lowest classified level.
w.3: E108 has no Class D.

mock2.q: How is felt underlayment normally applied on a 6:12 asphalt-shingle roof (no special ice or low-slope conditions)?
o: Not required on 6:12 roofs
Two layers with 19-in laps
Vertically, from ridge to eave
A single layer applied shingle-fashion, parallel to the eave, with about 2-in head laps and offset end laps
mock2.e: For 4:12 and steeper, a single layer is applied parallel to the eave, shingle-fashion, with 2-in head laps and staggered end laps, per the code and the manufacturer.

w.0: Underlayment is required.
w.1: Two layers with 19-in laps is the method for 2:12 to below 4:12.
w.2: Vertical application creates laps that run water into the seams.

mock2.q: An installer uses 3-tab shingles turned upside down (tabs pointing up the roof) as the starter course. What is the main problem?
o: The factory sealant ends up in the wrong place to seal the first course, and the cutouts may leave gaps under it
There is no problem; this is the recommended method
They void the fire rating
Upside-down starters are heavier
mock2.e: A starter's purpose is to put sealant at the eave to bond the first course and to back the first course's cutouts. Flipping a 3-tab moves the sealant away from the eave edge. Use a purpose-made starter, or a 3-tab with the tabs removed.

w.1: Manufacturers call for starters with the sealant near the eave edge.
w.2: The fire rating isn't the issue.
w.3: Weight isn't the issue.

mock2.q: A crew installs laminated shingles by "racking" them straight up the roof in columns, instead of stair-stepping diagonally. What problem can this cause?
o: Improved ventilation
Faster sealing
Better wind resistance
Visible color shading patterns, plus installation that may violate the manufacturer's instructions
mock2.e: Many manufacturers discourage or prohibit racking. It can produce visible shading and banding and alter offset and fastener patterns. Diagonal application is recommended.

w.0: Racking doesn't affect ventilation.
w.1: Racking doesn't affect sealing.
w.2: Racking doesn't improve wind resistance.

mock2.q: A new roof shows patches of slightly different shingle color. What is the most likely installation cause?
o: Bundles from different production lots were used or weren't blended
The attic was over-ventilated
The nails were too long
The underlayment was too thin
mock2.e: Color can vary between production runs. Using bundles from the same lot, and pulling from several bundles as you go, avoids visible patches.

w.1: Ventilation doesn't create color patches.
w.2: Nail length doesn't affect color.
w.3: Underlayment doesn't affect the visible color.

mock2.q: Asphalt shingles are being installed over ⅜-in plywood sheathing. How far must the nails penetrate?
o: ½ in into the sheathing
Exactly ¾ in, even if the nail doesn't reach through
Through the sheathing, because it is thinner than ¾ in
Only through the shingle and underlayment
mock2.e: Nails must penetrate at least ¾ in into the deck or through the deck, whichever is less. With ⅜-in sheathing, the nail must go completely through it.

w.0: ½ in doesn't meet the rule.
w.1: ¾-in penetration isn't possible in a ⅜-in deck. The rule is ¾ in or through.
w.3: The nails must engage the deck.

mock2.q: A pneumatic nailer is set too high, driving nail heads into the shingles. What is the main consequence?
o: The nail head cuts the mat and reduces holding power, making blow-offs more likely
The nails can't rust
Nothing; deeper is always better
The shingles seal faster
mock2.e: Overdriven nails break through the shingle and lose their ability to hold it. Nails should be driven flush with the shingle surface.

w.1: Rust isn't the concern here.
w.2: Nails must be flush, not driven deep.
w.3: Overdriving doesn't speed sealing.

mock2.q: How do NRCA and many shingle manufacturers regard staples for fastening asphalt shingles?
o: NRCA doesn't recommend them, and many manufacturers limit warranties, especially wind coverage, when staples are used
Staples are required in high-wind areas
Staples are preferred over nails
Staples are required on steep slopes
mock2.e: Staples are easily misapplied (crooked, over- or under-driven) and hold less reliably. NRCA doesn't recommend them, and many manufacturers restrict warranty coverage when they are used.

w.1: High-wind areas call for more nails, not staples.
w.2: Nails are the preferred fastener.
w.3: Steep slopes call for nails plus hand-sealing.

mock2.q: Fifteen-year-old shingles on a house with a poorly ventilated attic are curling and cupping far more than identical shingles on a well-ventilated garage. What is the most likely contributing cause?
o: Too much underlayment
Excess heat and moisture from the poorly ventilated attic
Starter strips at the eaves
Drip edge at the rakes
mock2.e: Heat and moisture building up under the deck speed shingle aging and distortion. The ventilated garage, with the same shingles, shows that the attic conditions are the difference.

w.0: Underlayment doesn't cause curling.
w.2: Starter strips don't cause curling.
w.3: Drip edge doesn't cause curling.

mock2.src: Shingle manufacturer ventilation requirements; NRCA ventilation practice

mock2.q: Soon after installation, long wavy ridges appear across a new shingle roof. It was installed the day after rain soaked the felt. What is the most likely cause?
o: High nailing
Algae growth
Too few ridge vents
Wrinkled or wet underlayment and deck moisture movement telegraphing through the shingles
mock2.e: When wet felt or sheathing is covered, the underlayment wrinkles and the panels move as they dry. The distortion shows through the shingles as buckling.

w.0: High nailing causes blow-offs, not waves.
w.1: Algae causes dark streaks.
w.2: Ventilation deficiencies cause long-term aging, not immediate buckling after a wet install.

mock2.q: Black streaks appear on the north slope of a shingle roof. What is the cause, and what is a common preventive measure?
o: Soot from the chimney; install a cricket
Asphalt bleeding from overheating; replace the roof
Mold rotting the deck; replace the sheathing
Algae growth; algae-resistant shingles or copper or zinc strips near the ridge
mock2.e: Dark streaks are typically algae (*Gloeocapsa magma*), a cosmetic problem. Algae-resistant granules, or copper and zinc strips that release inhibiting ions in runoff, help prevent it.

w.0: A cricket doesn't address algae.
w.1: Streaks aren't asphalt bleeding.
w.2: Surface algae isn't deck rot.

mock2.q: In an open metal valley, how is the exposed width typically laid out?
o: It narrows toward the eave to speed water flow
It is the same width from top to bottom
It widens toward the eave (commonly about ⅛ in per ft) so that water and debris flow freely
It is 0 in at the eave
mock2.e: Widening the open portion toward the eave handles the increasing water volume and lets ice and debris pass freely. The shingle edges are trimmed along chalk lines.

w.0: Narrowing toward the eave concentrates the water where the flow is greatest.
w.1: A constant width is sometimes used, but the common recommendation is to widen it.
w.3: A zero-width eave closes the valley.

mock2.q: An open valley is lined with mineral-surfaced roll roofing. How is it installed under the model code?
o: Roll roofing isn't permitted in valleys
A single 12-in strip, granules up
An 18-in-wide bottom layer (granules down), then a 36-in-wide top layer (granules up)
A 36-in bottom layer and an 18-in top layer, both granules up
mock2.e: The code method for mineral-surfaced roll roofing valleys is two layers: an 18-in bottom layer placed granules down, then a 36-in top layer granules up.

w.0: Roll roofing is a listed valley lining.
w.1: A single 12-in strip is too narrow and lacks the second layer.
w.3: The layer widths and orientation are reversed.

mock2.q: How is the valley underlayment sequenced with the field underlayment?
o: The field underlayment goes first, and the valley strip on top
A 36-in-wide valley underlayment or ice barrier is centered in the valley first, and the field underlayment then laps over it
The valley strip is installed after the shingles
No underlayment goes in valleys
mock2.e: The valley lining goes on first, centered in the valley. The field underlayment from each plane laps over it, so water in the field flows over the valley layer, not under it.

w.0: Field underlayment first would place the valley strip's edges where water can run under them.
w.2: Underlayment always goes under the shingles.
w.3: Valleys carry the most water and need underlayment.

mock2.q: Shingles are laid at a 5-in exposure. What is a typical length for each step flashing piece?
o: 4 in
5 in
7 in
12 in
mock2.e: Each step flashing piece should be about 2 in longer than the exposure, so each piece laps the one below by about 2 in. For a 5-in exposure, that's about 7 in. The code minimum leg dimension is 4 × 4 in.

w.0: 4 in is the code minimum leg dimension, not the length needed for a 5-in exposure.
w.1: 5 in equals the exposure and leaves no lap.
w.3: 12 in is longer than needed.

mock2.src: NRCA and manufacturer practice; IRC R905.2.8.3 [JURISDICTION]

mock2.q: What is the preferred way to flash a new curb-mounted skylight on a shingle roof?
o: Use a single piece of L-flashing around the whole curb
Rely on the skylight's gasket
Surround the skylight with roof cement only
Use the skylight manufacturer's flashing kit, installed in the sequence the manufacturer specifies
mock2.e: Manufacturer flashing kits use the correct laps, step flashing, and head and sill pieces for the unit, and are usually required to keep the warranty.

w.0: A continuous L-flashing at the sides lets water into the shingle laps.
w.1: A gasket doesn't replace roof flashing.
w.2: Cement alone is a temporary, maintenance-dependent fix.

mock2.q: A 25-ft aluminum panel run sees a 160°F temperature swing. Aluminum's coefficient is 12.8 × 10⁻⁶ in/in/°F. What is the approximate total movement?

w.0: 0.23 in comes from a unit or arithmetic error.
w.1: 0.31 in uses steel's coefficient (6.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 300 × 160 = 0.312 in), not aluminum's.
w.3: 1.23 in is about double the correct value.

mock2.q: In which direction are hip cap shingles installed?
o: Starting at the eave (bottom) and working up toward the ridge
Starting at the ridge and working down to the eave
From the middle of the hip outward
In either direction
mock2.e: Hips are capped from the bottom up, so each upper cap laps over the one below, following the water-shedding rule.

w.1: Top-down laps face uphill and catch water.
w.2: Working from the middle creates reverse laps.
w.3: Direction matters for the laps.

mock2.q: A house has one layer of flat, sound, dry 3-tab shingles and no deck problems. The owner wants a re-cover. Which statement is correct?
o: A re-cover is allowed over any number of layers
A re-cover is never allowed
A re-cover requires removing the underlayment first
A re-cover is generally allowed by the model codes, with fasteners long enough to penetrate the deck ¾ in or through it
mock2.e: Model codes generally allow one re-cover over a single sound layer of asphalt shingles. Nails must be longer to reach the deck. NRCA still prefers tear-off, but re-cover is a legal option.

w.0: Two or more existing layers prohibits a re-cover.
w.1: A single sound layer can usually be re-covered.
w.2: You can't remove the underlayment without removing the shingles.

mock2.q: An attic is 1,500 sq ft, and the 1/150 ratio applies. What total net free ventilation area is required?
o: 720 sq in
1,000 sq in
1,440 sq in
2,160 sq in

w.0: 720 sq in is the 1/300 amount.
w.1: 1,000 sq in confuses sq ft with sq in.
w.3: 2,160 sq in doesn't match either ratio.

mock2.q: Blown insulation is being added to an attic with soffit vents. What must be maintained at the eaves?
o: Plastic sheeting stapled over the soffit vents
The soffit vents packed with insulation to stop drafts
Nothing; blown insulation doesn't affect ventilation
Baffles (vent chutes) that keep insulation out of the soffit vents and keep an air space (at least 1 in under the model code) below the roof sheathing
mock2.e: Insulation must not block the intake vents. Baffles maintain a clear airflow channel from the soffit to the attic. The model code requires at least 1 in of space between the insulation and the roof sheathing at the vent.

w.0: Covering the vents stops airflow.
w.1: Blocking the intake stops the ventilation.
w.2: Blown insulation commonly blocks soffit vents.

mock2.q: Frost and mold are found on the attic sheathing directly above where a bathroom exhaust fan discharges into the attic. What is the correct fix?
o: Add an ice barrier at the eaves
Duct the fan to the exterior through a proper roof or wall cap
Add more attic insulation over the fan
Install a larger fan that still discharges into the attic
mock2.e: Exhaust fans must discharge to the outdoors. Dumping warm, moist air into a cold attic causes condensation, frost, and mold on the sheathing.

w.0: An ice barrier doesn't address attic moisture.
w.2: Insulation doesn't remove the moisture source.
w.3: A larger fan into the attic worsens the problem.

mock2.src: IRC M1501.1 / R303.3 [JURISDICTION]; NRCA ventilation practice

mock2.q: A contractor in northern Illinois uses the 1/300 ventilation ratio instead of 1/150. Which condition justifies it under the model code?
o: The house has a metal roof
The roof slope is 8:12 or steeper
At least 40% and not more than 50% of the required vent area is in the upper portion of the attic (within 3 ft of the ridge), and the rest is at the eaves
The attic has a powered fan
mock2.e: The 1/300 reduction applies when 40–50% of the vent area is high (within 3 ft of the ridge) and the balance is low (eave/soffit). The other route, a Class I or II ceiling vapor retarder, applies only in Climate Zones 6–8, and most of Illinois is Zone 4–5.

w.0: Roof material isn't a condition.
w.1: Slope isn't a condition.
w.3: Powered fans don't justify the reduction.

mock2.q: Concrete tile will be installed in a high-wind area. What governs how the tile is fastened (nails, clips, foam adhesive, wire-tie)?
o: Always one nail per tile regardless of wind
The tile manufacturer's installation instructions and the applicable code tables for the design wind speed
Mortar only, with no mechanical fastening
Whatever the crew prefers
mock2.e: Tile attachment depends on wind speed, roof height, slope, and product. Manufacturers and codes give fastening schedules that can include extra nails, clips, or approved foam adhesives.

w.0: One nail may be inadequate in high wind.
w.2: Mortar-only attachment is limited and often not allowed for wind resistance.
w.3: Crew preference isn't a specification.

mock2.src: Tile manufacturer/TRI installation guides; IRC R905.3 [JURISDICTION]

mock2.q: Where should a roofer step when walking on a concrete tile roof, to minimize breakage?
o: On the unsupported upper portion of the tile
Anywhere, since concrete tile is unbreakable
On the lower (headlap) portion of each tile, near the nose of the tile below, or on walk boards
On the ridge caps
mock2.e: A tile is best supported where it overlaps the tile below, at the headlap. Stepping on unsupported areas cracks tiles. Walk boards spread the load.

w.0: The unsupported area is where tiles break.
w.1: Concrete tile cracks under point loads.
w.3: Ridge caps are fragile and set in mortar or on nailers.

mock2.q: A single broken slate must be replaced on an otherwise sound slate roof. Which method is correct?
o: Remove the broken slate's nails with a slate ripper, then install the new slate secured with a slate hook, or a nail with a copper bib
Replace the entire roof section with asphalt shingles
Glue the broken pieces with roof cement
Face-nail the new slate through its center and caulk the nail head
mock2.e: A slate ripper cuts or pulls the hidden nails. The replacement slate is held by a slate hook, or by a nail in the joint above covered with a copper bib that sheds water.

w.1: Mixing asphalt shingles into a slate roof isn't a proper repair.
w.2: Glued slate fails and looks poor.
w.3: An exposed, caulked face nail is a future leak.

mock2.src: NRCA slate practice; slate industry repair guidance

mock2.q: How does the recommended slate headlap relate to roof slope?
o: Lower slopes need LESS headlap
Headlap is the same on all slopes
Lower slopes need MORE headlap; very steep slopes can use less
Headlap is only required on slopes over 20:12
mock2.e: Water moves more slowly on low slopes and can be driven farther up under the slates, so more headlap is used there (for example, about 4 in near 4:12 versus 3 in standard). On very steep slopes, headlap can be reduced.

w.0: That's the reverse of the principle.
w.1: Headlap varies with slope.
w.3: Headlap is required on all slate roofs.

mock2.q: 16-in No. 1 wood shingles are installed on a 5:12 roof. What is the maximum exposure under the common model-code table?
o: 3¾ in
5 in
5½ in
7½ in
mock2.e: For 16-in No. 1 wood shingles on slopes of 4:12 or more, the maximum exposure is 5 in. Between 3:12 and below 4:12 it drops to 3¾ in.

w.0: 3¾ in is the exposure for 3:12 to below 4:12.
w.2: 5½ in is for 18-in shingles at 4:12 and up.
w.3: 7½ in is for 24-in shingles at 4:12 and up.

mock2.src: IRC R905.7 wood shingle exposure table [JURISDICTION]

mock2.q: Which fastening practice is correct for wood shingles?
o: One electro-galvanized nail in the center of each shingle
Staples through the exposed face
Two corrosion-resistant fasteners (stainless or hot-dip galvanized) per shingle, about ¾ in from each edge, placed so the next course covers them
Four fasteners per shingle, exposed to the weather
mock2.e: Wood shingles take two fasteners each, about ¾ in from the edges and just above the exposure line, so the next course covers them. Stainless or hot-dip galvanized fasteners resist corrosion, including from the extractives in cedar.

w.0: One center nail lets the shingle split and cup.
w.1: Face staples are exposed and leak.
w.3: Fasteners must be concealed.

mock2.q: An owner wants metal roofing on a 1:12 porch roof. Which panel type is appropriate under the model code?
o: No metal roof is permitted on a 1:12 slope
Standing-seam panels, which are permitted down to ¼:12
Metal shingles
Exposed-fastener lapped panels without sealant
mock2.e: Standing-seam panels are allowed down to ¼:12. Lapped panels without sealant need 3:12, and metal shingles need 3:12.

w.0: Standing-seam metal is allowed at 1:12.
w.2: Metal shingles need 3:12.
w.3: Lapped panels without sealant need 3:12. With sealant, ½:12.

mock2.q: A new flat-pan standing-seam roof shows waviness in the flat areas between seams. What is this called, and how is it usually minimized?
o: Blistering; minimized with vapor retarders
Ridging; minimized by staggering insulation joints
Oil canning; minimized with heavier gauge, striations or stiffening ribs, a flat substrate, and correct clip installation
Racking; minimized by installing panels diagonally
mock2.e: Oil canning is visible waviness in the flat pans of metal panels. It is mostly aesthetic. It is reduced by stiffer panels (heavier gauge, striations), a smooth substrate, and clips that aren't overtightened.

w.0: Blistering is a membrane defect.
w.1: Ridging is a BUR defect.
w.3: Racking is a shingle application term.

mock2.src: Metal panel manufacturer technical bulletins; NRCA metal practice

mock2.q: A shed roof slopes UP to meet a vertical wall (a headwall). How is this intersection flashed?
o: Step flashing, one piece per course
Roof cement troweled into the joint
A kickout flashing only
A continuous apron flashing, extending up the wall behind the cladding and down over the top shingle course, counterflashed by the wall covering
mock2.e: At a headwall, water runs straight at the wall. A continuous apron (head) flashing turns up the wall (commonly at least 4 in) and laps down over the top course (commonly at least 4 in). The wall covering or a counterflashing laps over its vertical leg.

w.0: Step flashing is for SIDEWALLS, where the roof slopes along the wall.
w.1: Cement alone is a maintenance-dependent patch, not a flashing.
w.2: Kickout flashing goes at the bottom end of a sidewall intersection.

mock2.src: NRCA steep-slope flashing practice; manufacturer instructions

mock2.q: A crew plans to set Galvalume (aluminum-zinc coated) steel flashing directly into fresh mortar at a masonry wall. What is the concern?
o: Mortar will not stick to any metal
There is no concern; Galvalume is compatible with all materials
Wet mortar and concrete are alkaline and attack the aluminum-zinc coating, so the metal should be isolated or a compatible metal used
Galvalume is too flexible to embed
mock2.e: Galvalume's aluminum-zinc coating is damaged by alkaline wet mortar, concrete, and plaster, and by contact with lead or copper. Isolate it with a compatible membrane or coating, or choose a metal suited to masonry contact.

w.0: Adhesion isn't the issue here.
w.1: Galvalume has known incompatibilities.
w.3: Stiffness isn't the issue.

mock2.q: A 10-year-old roof needs a new penetration flashing welded in. Which membrane type can generally be heat-welded after it is cleaned with the manufacturer's weathered-membrane cleaner?
o: Coal-tar BUR
Gravel-surfaced asphalt BUR
EPDM
A thermoplastic such as PVC or TPO
mock2.e: Thermoplastics soften with heat and can be welded even when aged, after proper cleaning and preparation. Some aged TPO may be harder to weld.

w.0: Coal tar isn't welded; it's repaired with compatible bitumen.
w.1: BUR isn't welded.
w.2: EPDM is a thermoset and can't be heat-welded; it uses tape or adhesive.

mock2.q: Before seaming or adhering, why do EPDM manufacturers typically want the sheet unrolled and left to relax for a period of time?
o: So fold wrinkles and packaging stresses relax, and the sheet lies flat before it is bonded
So the membrane can cure in the sun
So the adhesive can dry on the sheet
So the sheet will shrink to fit
mock2.e: EPDM ships folded and rolled. Letting it relax, often about 30 minutes per the manufacturer, reduces wrinkles and internal stress before it is locked in place.

w.1: EPDM is already cured at the factory.
w.2: No adhesive has been applied yet.
w.3: Relaxation isn't meant to shrink the sheet.

mock2.q: Where is uncured (semi-cured) EPDM flashing typically used?
o: At inside and outside corners and irregular shapes, where it must stretch and conform
As the main field membrane
Under ballast as a slip sheet
For long straight wall flashings only
mock2.e: Uncured EPDM stretches and conforms, which makes it suited to corners, pipe boots, and odd shapes. Cured EPDM is used for straight wall flashings.

w.1: The field membrane is cured EPDM.
w.2: Uncured EPDM isn't a slip sheet.
w.3: Straight walls use cured flashing.

mock2.q: Which statement about ballasted EPDM roof systems is MOST accurate?
o: They are recommended for the highest-wind locations with no limits
They typically use about 10–12 psf of stone or pavers, and are limited to low slopes and buildings able to carry the load
They can be used on any slope up to 6:12
They add no dead load
mock2.e: Ballasted systems rely on weight. They require structural capacity for about 10–12 psf of stone (more for pavers), are limited to low slopes (commonly 2:12 or less), and have wind-exposure limits.

w.0: Wind limits apply, because stone can scour or blow off.
w.2: Ballast slides off steeper slopes.
w.3: The ballast is substantial dead load.

mock2.src: EPDM manufacturer and FM/ANSI-SPRI RP-4 guidance

mock2.q: A contractor proposes installing only the base sheet and first ply on the whole roof this week, then returning a month later for the rest of the plies. Why does NRCA discourage this?
o: It is required in cold weather
It is faster and uses less asphalt
The plies bond better after weathering
Moisture, dirt, and dust collect between phases, causing poor adhesion, blisters, and delamination
mock2.e: Phased application leaves partly finished plies exposed. Moisture and contaminants get trapped between the phases and cause blistering and delamination. Plies should be finished continuously.

w.0: No such requirement exists.
w.1: Speed isn't the issue, and quality suffers.
w.2: Weathered plies bond worse.

mock2.q: A smooth-surfaced asphalt roof with no coating shows a network of deep surface cracks resembling alligator hide. What is the cause?
o: A poorly ventilated attic
UV and weathering have aged the unprotected asphalt, which shrinks and cracks
Trapped moisture between plies
Too much gravel
mock2.e: Exposed asphalt oxidizes under UV and heat, loses its oils, shrinks, and cracks in an alligator pattern. Surfacing or reflective coatings protect it.

w.0: Attic ventilation is a steep-slope residential issue.
